channel.description: Utah breaking news and local top stories from KSL.com

item.title: Road delays expected near Utah Capitol as work on new historic trail begins
item.description: UDOT will close State Street between North Temple and 300 North starting Monday through the end of November to build the Pioneer Trail near the Utah State Capitol, though the cross intersections will stay open. The agency is urging drivers to detour onto Main Street during the closure. Utah lawmakers approved $10 million this year to complete funding for the trail, adding to $5 million previously pledged by the This Is the Place Foundation. The finished 2-mile walking loop, inspired by Boston's Freedom Trail, will link historic sites such as Council Hall, Memory Grove and the Crismon Mill Site between the Capitol and the new Museum of Utah and Temple Square.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Saratoga Springs marks 25th anniversary of 9/11 with 3 days of community service
item.description: Saratoga Springs residents spent three days this week on service projects marking the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks, including a food and coat drive, meal-kit prep for a middle school pantry, and premature-baby clothing projects at Westlake High School led by volunteers such as Todd and Julia Wamboldt. City civic events coordinator Corrine Prestwich said the turnout reflects how communities rally when a need is identified, with more than 2,400 volunteers taking part last year and organizers hoping to top that this year. Westlake High School students also placed 2,977 flags representing each 9/11 victim ahead of a Friday assembly, and the city's observance continues with a free patriotic concert Friday evening at Neptune Park.
item.dc:creator: Garna Mejia, KSL

item.title: 2 more arrested in connection with South Salt Lake bank robbery
item.description: Salt Lake County booked two more men, Thomas Domingo Bustos, 31, and Fidel Ybarra, 52, on aggravated robbery and hoax-weapon-of-mass-destruction charges tied to a Sept. 4 robbery of an America First Credit Union branch in South Salt Lake, where a note claimed a bomb was present. Brelyn Capri Sanchez, 37, had already been arrested as the alleged getaway driver, and a police affidavit says surveillance and UTA camera footage tracked vehicles tied to Bustos moving between an apartment complex and the bank before and after the heist. Investigators say Bustos organized the plan and received the roughly $1,200 taken, corroborated by cellphone records, while Ybarra was identified as the man who handed the teller the note and later admitted the "bomb" was fake; it has not been recovered. Both Bustos and Sanchez were already on probation from prior convictions at the time of their arrests.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Comedian Jon Stewart has some questions for Utah's governor
item.description: Utah Gov. Spencer Cox appeared on "The Daily Show" to promote his new book on peacemaking, "Off Ramp," written in the aftermath of Charlie Kirk's assassination in Orem, and host Jon Stewart pressed him on whether his call to avoid contempt let genuinely contemptible acts go unchallenged, citing Sen. Mike Lee's deleted posts about a Minnesota lawmaker's killing. Cox responded that his book argues for confronting disagreement face-to-face rather than abandoning the ability to call things contemptible. Stewart also asked what Cox actually did to win President Trump's backing for $1 billion toward the Great Salt Lake, and Cox said he worked to keep the issue from being seen as a partisan cause. Stewart closed by thanking Cox for the good-faith exchange and recommending the book despite ribbing Utah's coffee culture.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: 'She didn't waste a moment': Manti father remembers wife, newborn son after tragic crash
item.description: Tyson Hafen spoke to KSL just days after his wife, Rebeca Hafen, and their newborn son died following a Tuesday crash near Manti in which a driver blinded by the sun struck her while she was walking; the baby was delivered by emergency C-section and died the next day. Hafen described his wife of 14 years as someone who lived every moment fully and loved raising and homeschooling their nine children, the oldest just 13. He said the family held and said goodbye to the newborn while he was on life support, and that he holds no anger toward the driver, believing the timing of life and death isn't in human hands. A GoFundMe for the family has raised more than $150,000.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL and Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: Why the strip is being flipped outside Utah Governor's Mansion
item.description: Crews removed the grass park strip between the Utah Governor's Mansion and South Temple and installed drip irrigation, with volunteers set to plant more than 1,800 water-wise, pollinator-friendly native plants, as first lady Abby Cox said the state wants to lead by example on conservation. A full-perimeter conversion of the mansion grounds is planned for next spring, part of Slow the Flow's "Week of Service," which also includes projects at the South Salt Lake Community Center, Coalville City Hall and Hyde Park City Hall. The push comes as over 90% of Utah remains in severe to exceptional drought, reservoirs sit at 50% capacity versus a normal 59%, and the Great Salt Lake's southern arm has fallen to its second-lowest recorded level. Slow the Flow director Tage Flint said state data show removing 1,000 square feet of park strip can save 27,000 gallons of water a year, with residential lawns accounting for 97% of municipal and industrial water use in the Great Salt Lake basin.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Clearfield leaders OK 180-day moratorium on data center development
item.description: The Clearfield City Council voted 4-0 Tuesday to bar new data center development for 180 days while officials study whether special zoning rules are needed, joining Box Elder, Iron and Cache counties in adopting similar pauses amid statewide debate over the industry's water and power use. City planner Tyson Stoddard said Clearfield's code has no definition or standards yet for data centers' electrical, water, noise and infrastructure demands, and no specific project is currently proposed in the city. Mayor Mark Shepherd, who also sits on the board that approved measures enabling the contested Stratos data center project in Box Elder County's Hansel Valley, said the moratorium lets Clearfield get ahead of the issue while the state develops its own statewide standards. The Stratos project, championed by businessman Kevin O'Leary, has drawn criticism over water and power use even as backers tout its economic and national-security benefits.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: 1 year later, some UVU students still affected by Charlie Kirk shooting
item.description: A year after Charlie Kirk was shot and killed at an outdoor event on the Utah Valley University campus, UVU student Josh Millward says the shock of that day still shapes students' grades, attendance and motivation, even for those who weren't eyewitnesses but got texts from friends checking in. Millward said the tragedy has become how outsiders identify UVU, and he hopes the school will eventually be known more for programs like entrepreneurship. UVU was closed Thursday for reflection, service and connection, and Turning Point USA held an anniversary memorial that evening at the UCCU Center, while the university's "Our Better Selves for a Better America" initiative continues to promote civil dialogue. Millward said political violence is wrong regardless of viewpoint and hopes the shooting becomes part of, but not the defining feature of, UVU's history.
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: Provo man charged with killing his aunt in Salem
item.description: Prosecutors charged Isaiah Christopher Ramos, 26, of Provo with murder, obstruction of justice and aggravated abuse of a vulnerable adult after his aunt, 70-year-old Carla Anderson, was found dead and stiff in her Salem home Aug. 31, despite his 911 call reporting her unresponsive. Charging documents say officers found blood near her mouth and a ransacked-looking house with expensive valuables untouched, and that Ramos stood to inherit half of Anderson's estate. Ramos told police he left on a road trip in his modified bus Aug. 27-30, but FLOCK camera hits placed his motorcycle in Santaquin overnight on Aug. 31, contradicting his claim he was alone the whole time, and investigators noted scratches on his arms he attributed to eczema. An autopsy found injuries consistent with strangulation and material under Anderson's fingernails now pending DNA testing.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: 'Modern-day martyr': Thousands honor Charlie Kirk at UVU memorial
item.description: Thousands attended a Turning Point USA memorial Thursday evening at UVU's UCCU Center marking one year since founder Charlie Kirk was fatally shot on campus, with keynote speaker Glenn Beck calling him a hero and Frank Turek, who was near Kirk when he was shot, calling him a "modern-day martyr." Other speakers, including commentators Michael Knowles and Turning Point's Andrew Sypher, argued Kirk's death has left American politics more divided, while Beck criticized dark conspiracy theories targeting Kirk's widow, Erika Kirk, and urged responding to hostility with grace. Tyler Robinson, 23, is charged with aggravated murder in Kirk's killing and has pleaded not guilty after a judge found sufficient evidence to send the case to trial; he could face the death penalty if convicted. The event mixed somber moments, including a moment of silence, with the energy of a political rally.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Sherry Black Foundation organizes special event for Utah cold case families
item.description: Heidi Miller, daughter of bookstore owner Sherry Black, who was stabbed to death in 2010, described in a new KSL COLD podcast bonus episode the years of "ambiguous grief" her family endured before investigative genetic genealogy led detective Ben Pender to identify and arrest killer Adam Durborow in 2020; he is now serving life without parole. Miller founded the Sherry Black Foundation in 2017 to train law enforcement and support families of missing or murdered people whose cases remain unsolved. The foundation is co-hosting the inaugural Utah Missing and Unsolved Day on Sept. 26 at Salt Lake Community College's Miller Campus in Sandy, where families can learn to get loved ones properly listed in cold-case databases, meet victim advocates and hear about new forensic techniques. Miller said the event's goal is to offer families the same hope that helped her survive years without answers.
item.dc:creator: Dave Cawley, KSL

item.title: Primary Children's behavioral health campus marks 1 year, nearly 10,000 kids served
item.description: Intermountain Primary Children's Behavioral Health Center in Taylorsville has served nearly 10,000 children and families in its first year, hospital president Amanda Choudhary said, citing strong community need for youth mental health care. Parent Megan Alsop described how her son Roman's eight-to-ten-week stay in the campus's Partial Hospitalization Program, with individual and group therapy from a multidisciplinary team, helped him return to a typical junior high a year later. The campus also runs a 24/7 walk-in crisis center that assistant service director Heather Shotwell said has served about 1,100 children and adolescents, letting families get assessed and build safety plans instead of resorting to emergency rooms or police. Shotwell said parents don't need to wait for a crisis to seek help, and families can also reach the Primary Children's Stabilization and Mobile Response team through 988.
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: Judge declines to pause Utah's prop betting law, pending appeal
item.description: A pair of 10th Circuit Court of Appeals judges denied prediction-market company Kalshi's request for an emergency injunction to block Utah's new ban on proposition betting while its broader appeal proceeds, ruling the company hadn't shown the necessary factors favored it. Kalshi, regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, argues its "event contracts" aren't subject to state gambling law, but U.S. District Judge Robert Shelby ruled last month that federal commodities law doesn't preempt Utah's constitutional gambling ban. Utah had countered that Kalshi was unlikely to win on appeal and wouldn't suffer irreparable harm without a pause. The ruling means Utah can continue enforcing its prop-betting ban as the underlying appeal moves forward; Kalshi did not immediately comment.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: UDOT tries a new approach to address its beaver problem in Logan Canyon
item.description: The Utah Department of Transportation has installed three "pond leveler" pipes along Beaver Creek in Logan Canyon, aiming to let beavers keep building dams naturally without flooding U.S. 89, after years of trapping and relocating beavers only to see new ones move in. Natural resources manager Matt Howard said the levelers quietly drain excess water through the dams before it reaches road-damaging levels, letting beavers stay in place instead of seeking new spots to dam. UDOT developed the approach with the Division of Wildlife Resources, Sageland Collaborative and Utah State University's Beaver Ecology and Relocation Collaborative; Sageland's Shane Hill said keeping more water in the canyon can also improve water quality and fire resistance. Officials plan to monitor the levelers' performance and could expand the approach elsewhere in Utah if it works.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: UVU president says independent findings from Kirk assassination to be released this month
item.description: New Utah Valley University President Jon Anderson, who started the job in August after previously leading PennWest University, told KSL that an independent outside review of last year's Charlie Kirk shooting, including findings and recommendations, will be released later this month. Anderson said the university has since formed a major events safety assessment committee, launched safety training for faculty, staff and students, and strengthened ties with local and state law enforcement to respond faster to future incidents. He noted only six police officers were on duty for the crowd of thousands at the event where Kirk was shot, according to courtroom testimony. Anderson said UVU will not shy away from what happened but doesn't want the tragedy to define the university's future.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Kirk support at USU continues to grow in year after his death
item.description: Utah State University Turning Point USA chapter leaders Kaitlin Griffiths and Ethan Harper traveled to UVU to help set up Thursday's memorial for Charlie Kirk, pausing their work at 12:23 p.m., the moment Kirk was shot a year earlier. Griffiths, the chapter's president, said membership has grown from about 50 to more than 250 since Kirk's death, calling the tragedy a uniting moment for the conservative movement despite its horror. Harper, the chapter's vice president, said he had a ticket to Kirk's UVU event but skipped it, and that the aftermath pulled him from political disinterest into organizing protests, speaking events and voter registration drives. Both said they see their growing activism as carrying forward what they believe Kirk would have wanted.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: Groups reflect on political division 1 year After Charlie Kirk's Death
item.description: A year after Charlie Kirk's killing at UVU, civic groups including Braver Angels are urging Americans to move past viewing political opponents as enemies, with Braver Angels CEO Maury Giles warning that framing disagreement as "I'm good, you're evil" erodes the country's social fabric. Speakers at a recent Utah County discussion said lowering the temperature of political discourse starts with individuals taking personal responsibility rather than assuming rival "tribes" are under threat. Advocates argued that declining interaction between people of different political views lets stereotypes and assumptions fill the gap, and that the goal isn't to change anyone's beliefs but to foster curiosity over hostility. Organizers said the anniversary is a reminder that preserving civil discourse begins with individuals choosing to listen and seek common ground.
item.dc:creator: Annette Campbell, KSL

item.title: 2 students with special needs abandoned on Tooele school bus
item.description: Two Tooele County elementary students with special needs, including 7-year-old Winston Prawitt, were left alone for about 10 minutes on a school bus parked in direct sunlight at a district transportation yard Aug. 24 after a substitute driver on a special-education route failed to complete required drop-off procedures. Parents Travis and Alaina Prawitt say they learned something was wrong when the school confirmed Winston never arrived, then found him roughly five miles away at the bus yard; surveillance footage showed both boys screaming and pounding on the windows and doors. District spokesperson Brett Valdez confirmed the substitute driver didn't follow transportation procedures, and staff located and transported the students to school once notified. The Prawitts are now calling for new statewide school bus safety requirements, saying the outcome could have been far worse had they not noticed quickly.
item.dc:creator: Garna Mejia, KSL

item.title: Man admits to killing estranged girlfriend, a local Spanish radio host, almost five years ago
item.description: Manuel Omar Burciaga Perea, 39, pleaded guilty Thursday to murder, domestic violence in the presence of a child, and reckless endangerment for fatally shooting his estranged girlfriend, Spanish-language radio host Gabriela "Gaby" Sifuentes Castilla, 38, at her home on Oct. 17, 2021. The plea deal reduced the original aggravated murder charge and dropped aggravated burglary and assault counts; prosecutor Karissa McKinney said it secures accountability while sparing Sifuentes' young daughter from testifying about "the most traumatic event of her life." Sifuentes' sister, Rocio Sifuentes, testified she initially approved the deal but has since withdrawn her support, though prosecutors are standing by it. Burciaga was charged in November 2021 but wasn't arraigned until 2023 after being arrested in Mexico and extradited; his sentencing is scheduled for Dec. 10.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Court rejects Ute Tribe bid for ownership of 1.5 million acres that remain part of Utah reservation
item.description: A unanimous panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit has rejected the Ute Indian Tribe's bid to reclaim ownership of roughly 1.5 million acres within the Uncompahgre Reservation in eastern Utah, affirming a lower court ruling that favored the federal government and the state of Utah. The court found the tribe lacks "compensable title" to the land, meaning it isn't eligible for restoration under the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934, even though the reservation itself remains intact and the tribe retains jurisdiction there. BYU law professor Michalyn Steele told KSL the ruling is a narrow, technical decision about land title rather than a stripping of tribal authority. The dispute traces back to the tribe's 2016 request that the Department of the Interior restore the land, which Interior denied before the tribe unsuccessfully challenged that decision in court.
item.dc:creator: Eric Cabrera, KSL

item.title: Commission delays housing proposal vote that has Salt Lake City residents split
item.description: The Salt Lake City Planning Commission postponed a vote Wednesday on a citywide rezoning proposal called "expanding housing options" because of a scheduling error, pushing the decision to its next meeting later this month even as residents on both sides argued their case. The plan would let landowners build smaller single-family homes, duplexes, triplexes, fourplexes and four-unit townhomes on smaller lots across six residential zones covering about 33,000 properties, more than a third of the city's land and three-quarters of its residentially zoned land, while capping heights at 30 feet. Senior city planner Andy Hulka said the modest zoning tweaks are meant to ease Salt Lake City's rising housing costs, which a University of Utah Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute report released the same day pegged at a $565,000 median single-family home price, up nearly 8% year over year and the seventh-highest among Utah cities of at least 40,000 residents. That report also found 91% of Utah renters statewide are now priced out of homeownership.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Utah's high altitude and high suicide rate warrant further discussion, clinicians agree
item.description: Local clinicians who make up the Greater Utah Child Neuropsychology Education Group met Wednesday to revisit a 2018 University of Utah study linking the state's high elevation to its above-average rates of depression and suicide. Psychologist Sari Soutor Farhart said the group wanted a clearer answer for why life in Utah can feel difficult despite its natural beauty, and to pass that understanding on to clients. The review, published in the Harvard Review of Psychiatry by University of Utah psychiatrist Brent M. Kious along with Douglas G. Kondo and Perry F. Renshaw, points to hypoxia, or reduced oxygen at altitude, as a factor that may impair serotonin production and the brain's energy efficiency, both mechanisms tied to depression. Kious noted that at Salt Lake City's roughly 4,300-foot elevation, residents already live with somewhat lower oxygen levels than people near sea level, though he stressed altitude is only one of many contributing factors.
item.dc:creator: Brenna Donnelly, KSL

item.title: Roy man faces multiple charges for alleged sexual activity with three girls
item.description: Weber County prosecutors filed 18 charges Wednesday against 23-year-old David Isai Soriano of Roy, accusing him of providing three 13-year-old girls with THC vape products, nicotine and alcohol in exchange for sexual activity in Riverdale during July and August. The charges include four first-degree felony counts of rape of a child, three of aggravated sexual abuse of a child and two of sodomy on a child, along with lesser counts of enticing a minor, sexual exploitation of a minor, drug distribution in a drug-free zone and furnishing alcohol to a minor. Charging documents say Riverdale police learned of the allegations in August after the girls reported trading sexual acts for vapes and other substances, including one encounter described as occurring in a church parking lot. Soriano reportedly admitted to the conduct and was being held without bail in the Weber County Jail as of Wednesday.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor's surprise visit inspires students
item.description: U.S. Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor made a secret two-day visit last Thursday and Friday to schools across the Jordan School District in the West Jordan area, a trip kept hidden from the public and media until it concluded. The visit stemmed from a video invitation Jordan School District students sent Sotomayor more than a year ago, which she accepted; during her stay she met with students, teachers and administrators and encouraged them to pursue their goals. Fort Herriman Middle School ninth grader Breklyn Kollman, 14, presented a Freedom of Speech argument to the justice as part of a "We The People" competition and said Sotomayor personally told her she should attend law school. Riverton High School student body president Carson Davis, who had lunch with Sotomayor, described her as unusually personal and engaged with students about their schoolwork.
item.dc:creator: Dan Rascon, KSL

item.title: Man in Millcreek in custody after shots fired
item.description: A man was taken into custody Wednesday night in Millcreek after Unified police say he fired shots at officers responding to a domestic violence call on Lambourne Avenue. Police said a relative at the home reported the man, who was armed with a rifle, during an argument, and after assessing the situation officers determined he was suicidal and pulled back, calling in drones to monitor the area. The man then fired at officers before fleeing on foot through the neighborhood still carrying the rifle, prompting a reverse 911 alert telling residents within three miles to shelter in place. He was later located and arrested without further incident, and police said no one was injured.
item.dc:creator: Devin Oldroyd, KSL

item.title: Charges filed against man accused of ramming police car, stealing child's scooter
item.description: Midvale prosecutors charged 39-year-old Jeffrey David Levie on Tuesday with assault on a police officer, burglary and several other counts after he allegedly rammed a patrol car while fleeing in a stolen Honda Civic on Sept. 2. Charging documents say Levie backed and sped through a parking lot near 50 West and 7200 South, rammed an officer's vehicle when police tried to stop him, then drove roughly 45 mph through condominium backyards before crashing through a fence into a tree. After the crash, he allegedly ran into a nearby home and stole a child's scooter, helmet and T-shirt to disguise himself, and was arrested a short time later near a canal trail still wearing the child's shirt and carrying the scooter. Prosecutors say Levie has 28 prior arrests, including 13 convictions and four felonies, for offenses such as theft and burglary.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: The barcode is changing: What 'Sunrise 2027' means for Utah shoppers
item.description: An industry-wide effort called "Sunrise 2027" aims to have retail checkout systems capable of reading new two-dimensional barcodes alongside traditional UPC codes by the end of 2027, according to GS1, the nonprofit that has managed barcode standards since the UPC's debut in the 1970s. GS1 US senior vice president Melanie Nuce-Hilton told KSL's Matt Gephardt that unlike a UPC, the new codes can carry details such as lot numbers and expiration dates, potentially letting stores flag aging food, mark it down or block a recalled batch at checkout, while also linking shoppers to ingredient, allergen and recycling information. Gephardt and KSL executive producer Sloan Schrage found some Salt Lake City products already carrying QR codes, though scanning them mostly surfaced the same nutrition information already on the label. Nuce-Hilton said the bigger long-term benefit is letting shoppers "unlock the product story" in the aisle, from dietary details to instant recipes.
item.dc:creator: Matt Gephardt and Sloan Schrage, KSL

item.title: Get Outside Utah provides southern Utah teens the opportunity to get outside
item.description: The southern Utah nonprofit Get Outside, founded in 2020 by Matt Mizukawa and his wife, took a group of high school students canyoneering in Ghost Rider Canyon in the Virgin River Gorge along the Utah-Arizona line this week, giving many their first taste of outdoor recreation. Mizukawa said the organization, which has served more than 4,000 southern Utah high schoolers through clubs offering activities like rock climbing, mountain biking, kayaking and skiing, exists to remove the cost and access barriers that kept him from similar activities growing up in Maryland before his family moved to St. George. Hurricane High School student Zoey Mecham rappelled into the canyon for the first time on the trip, calling the experience "so cool" and saying she'd long wanted to try such activities but lacked the resources. Mizukawa said the outdoors changed his own life at 16 and that he and his wife started Get Outside to share that experience with as many youth as possible.
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: Utah Supreme Court justice recuses himself from Planned Parenthood lawsuit over abortion ban
item.description: Utah Supreme Court Justice John Nielsen has recused himself from an upcoming appeal in Planned Parenthood Association of Utah's long-running challenge to the state's abortion trigger law, clearing the way for a lower court judge to hear arguments next month instead. Nielsen, appointed to the court last year, had previously filed a friend-of-the-court brief for Pro-Life Utah in the case in 2022 while working as a private attorney; Planned Parenthood asked the court in July to disqualify him on those grounds, and Nielsen initially resisted before voluntarily stepping aside last week. Planned Parenthood Association of Utah president and CEO Shireen Ghorbani said in a statement that the recusal rules are clear and that she appreciated Nielsen's decision. The underlying case dates to a 2020 Utah law banning abortion with few exceptions, which briefly took effect in 2022 after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade before a district judge issued a preliminary injunction halting it.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Trump Justice Department says it's investigating Utah's lieutenant governor
item.description: The U.S. Department of Justice's Civil Rights Division has told Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson she is under investigation for allegedly failing to comply with federal voter-record laws after she refused to hand over the state's voter rolls, according to a letter Henderson posted on social media Wednesday. Henderson, a Republican, responded on Threads that she hadn't previously been told of the investigation and accused the DOJ of "baselessly harassing election officials" instead of focusing on real problems. The department said it sent similar letters to states currently in active litigation over noncompliance with voter list requests, following a July threat of possible criminal prosecution against Henderson; courts have rejected more than 20 similar federal lawsuits against states seeking such data. Utah House Minority Leader Angela Romero, a Salt Lake City Democrat, publicly thanked Henderson for resisting the request, a rare cross-party show of support given many Republican leaders' reluctance to challenge the Trump administration's election-data push.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Pregnant mother of 9, baby from Manti die in auto-pedestrian accident
item.description: Rebeca Hafen, 34, of Manti died after being struck by a vehicle while walking Tuesday morning near 1808 E. Dairy Lane just north of Moroni in Sanpete County, with the Utah Highway Patrol citing sun glare as the main factor in the crash. Hafen was pregnant with her ninth child at the time, and doctors performed an emergency delivery after she was taken to the hospital, but the newborn, who had been placed in the NICU, died Wednesday, according to updates from a GoFundMe campaign set up for the family. The fundraiser organizer said Hafen's husband, Tyson, and the couple's children were able to hold and say goodbye to the baby before he died. The GoFundMe, which had raised more than $80,000 as of Wednesday, is intended to help the family cover medical costs and care for the surviving children in the aftermath.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Former SLC fire battalion chief sentenced to jail, probation on child pornography charges
item.description: Kelly J. Carter, 52, a former Salt Lake City fire battalion chief who retired in December after being hired in 2000, was sentenced Aug. 11 to a year in jail and four years of probation for sexual exploitation of a minor after pleading guilty in May. Third District Judge Chelsea Koch suspended a one-to-15-year prison term, giving Carter credit for six months already served; he had originally faced 10 counts before pleading guilty to one under a plea deal. Charging documents say the case began with a tip to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children about a cryptocurrency payment tied to a child sexual abuse material website, and that Carter admitted buying a subscription and viewing the material on his iPhone while at work. A search of his phone turned up hundreds of images, some dating to 2020, with charges alleging he had viewed such material for at least six years; as part of probation he must complete inpatient treatment and cannot access the internet without approval.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Doctor shares survival story as U of U Health celebrates 25 years as Level I trauma center
item.description: University of Utah Health marked 25 years as Utah's first Level I trauma center on Wednesday, an anniversary made personal when Dr. Thomas Higgins, the hospital's chief of orthopedic trauma surgery, publicly shared for the first time that he was treated there after a near-fatal backcountry skiing accident. Higgins said he fell more than 100 feet onto granite and ice while trying to traverse Cardiff Pass with his wife on Dec. 30, 2025, suffering severe hypothermia and a serious head injury before his wife flagged down help and an air medical crew flew him to the hospital. He described having to relearn how to walk during his recovery and said he was, for the first time, able to personally thank the Intermountain Healthcare Life Flight crew that helped save him. Hospital chief operating officer Dan Lundergan called the anniversary a "remarkable time," while trauma medical director Toby Enniss noted the center serves the largest geographic catchment area of any trauma center in the contiguous United States, spanning Utah, Idaho, Wyoming and parts of Montana, Nevada and Colorado.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: Former Utah National Guard accountant accused of pocketing money from services program
item.description: Utah prosecutors charged 55-year-old Mark Daniel Oleson of West Haven on Tuesday with communications fraud, theft and multiple tax counts, accusing the former Utah National Guard accountant of pocketing more than $200,000 meant for the Guard's Morale, Welfare and Recreation program. Charging documents say the State Bureau of Investigation began looking into Oleson after he resigned from the program in 2024, when questions arose over Venmo payments for RV storage rent that were meant for the program but landed in his personal account, ultimately 53 such payments according to investigators. Investigators also found 203 ATM cash deposits to Oleson's account between 2021 and 2024 totaling more than $190,000, with 165 of those deposits made the same day as Morale, Welfare and Recreation program deposits. Notably, 162 of the deposits were made at an ATM in Saratoga Springs near Camp Williams, roughly 70 miles from Oleson's home in West Haven, according to the charges.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: With Pineview Reservoir emptying, pipeline project expected to proceed next week
item.description: With Pineview Reservoir largely drained, Ogden officials say preliminary work to build a solid berm across the exposed lakebed, the first step toward installing a new water pipeline section, is set to begin next week. Ogden public services director Justin Anderson told the City Council Tuesday that the berm will give crews a stable base to lay new piping parallel to an aging section that currently carries drinking water from a well field near Pineview through Ogden Canyon to the city, part of a broader $100 million project replacing 6.4 miles of pipeline serving about 120,000 Ogden-area customers. Anderson said the reservoir crossing should be finished by January, even though the overall pipeline project isn't due to wrap up until spring 2029, with incentives in place for the contractor to work 20 to 24 hours a day, six days a week. The reservoir's drawdown, which had it at 17% of normal capacity last week and headed toward below 2%, was driven partly by last winter's low snowpack and dry conditions.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Northrop Grumman, Utah officials unveil new facility that will aid in B-21 production
item.description: Northrop Grumman formally unveiled a new 845,000-square-foot facility called East Gate 3 in Layton, next to Hill Air Force Base, on Wednesday to support production of the B-21 Raider stealth bomber. Corporate vice president Tom Jones said the first completed B-21 should be delivered next year to Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota, its first operational base, while B-21 division vice president Chris Adams said only that "key components" of the aircraft will be built at the Utah site. The Air Force has requested a minimum of 100 of the bombers, which Air Force estimates put at an average unit cost of about $692 million in 2022 dollars, and Jones and Adams both described the program as central to future U.S. deterrence. The Layton facility is expected to employ up to 1,500 people in engineering and manufacturing roles by 2032, and Utah Senate President Stuart Adams and Layton Mayor Joy Petro joined Northrop Grumman officials at the ribbon-cutting ceremony.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Utah-based 'i love you, bro' project using love, camaraderie to combat high male suicide rates
item.description: A Lehi-based support network called "i love you, bro" is holding weekly small-group meetings across Utah to help men build connection and cope with mental health struggles, in response to data showing men die by suicide at far higher rates than women. Founder Joe Tuia'ana started the nonprofit in 2022 after talking a man down from a freeway overpass and then finding no follow-up resources existed for him. The project now runs 15 groups statewide offering evidence-based workshops, which organizers describe as the only program of its kind nationally. University of Utah Zero Suicide Program medical director Dr. Eric Monson said men often face unique barriers to seeking mental health care, and participants say the peer support has given them space to be vulnerable.
item.dc:creator: Brian Carlson, KSL

item.title: Scheduled end of protected status for Salvadoran immigrants draws fire from Utah advocates
item.description: Federal Temporary Protected Status for roughly 170,000 Salvadorans nationwide is set to expire Wednesday, alarming Utah's Salvadoran community even as the Department of Homeland Security signaled to KSL that a final decision hadn't yet been announced. Gladis Rodriguez, a Utah-based Salvadoran community leader, said many recipients have built lives, jobs and businesses in the U.S. and are reluctant to return to El Salvador. South Jordan immigration attorney Carlos Trujillo and West Valley City attorney Ysabel Lonazco criticized the move, noting Salvadoran TPS holders have lived in the U.S. since the designation was created after 2001 earthquakes. About 2,000 of Utah's roughly 20,000 Salvadoran residents are believed to hold TPS status, and attorneys expect a supervision-then-removal process similar to what followed the end of Haitian TPS in July.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Woman given consecutive sentence after judge calls treatment of her mother 'torture'
item.description: A 3rd District judge sentenced Lori Meers, 54, to two consecutive one-to-15-year prison terms after a jury convicted her of manslaughter and aggravated abuse of a vulnerable adult in the death of her 77-year-old mother. Judge Coral Sanchez called Meers' treatment of her mother "torture," citing video and photo evidence showing the woman left in unsanitary conditions and being verbally abused. The mother, identified in court records by the initials W.P., died in March 2025 of septic shock from acute pancreatitis after living in Meers' care despite other resources being available. Meers faces between two and 30 years behind bars.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Creekstone Energy, University of Utah studying feasibility of novel water generation technology
item.description: Creekstone Energy, developer of the planned Delta Gigasite data center campus in Millard County, announced a patent-pending technology called GIGAWATER aimed at capturing water vapor from natural-gas-fired electricity generation and converting it into usable water. CEO Ray Conley said the still-conceptual system is meant to address concerns that massive data centers will strain Utah's already drought-stressed water supply. Creekstone has signed a research agreement with the University of Utah's Energy and Geoscience Institute — funded entirely by Creekstone — to independently test the concept's core assumptions around chemistry, heat transfer and expected water recovery at the scale of the Delta Gigasite.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Vernal mother accused of child abuse after leaving children home alone
item.description: A Vernal woman, 28-year-old Lilian Sofia Ochoa Orizabal, faces two counts of reckless aggravated child abuse after prosecutors say she left her two young children, ages 3 and 6, home alone with a stove on. Court documents say the children ran from their smoke-filled apartment on July 25 screaming for their mother, and a neighbor who responded found burnt food and heavy smoke but no adults present. Orizabal reportedly told police she had gone to the store and left the children with a cellphone, returning about 45 minutes after officers arrived.
item.dc:creator: Heather Peterson, KSL

item.title: Utah family details extreme weather, chaos witnessed during Hurricane Lowell
item.description: A Saratoga Springs family's Hawaii vacation turned frightening when Hurricane Lowell bore down on Kauai during their stay, forcing last-minute scrambles for supplies. Madison Currey said the family wasn't worried at first since early forecasts showed the storm moving away, but concern grew as it turned back toward the islands, leading to long lines at Costco and a two-hour wait at the gas station. Lowell was the third tropical system to threaten Hawaii in weeks amid an active Pacific hurricane season, following Hurricane Lala's flooding of the Big Island in mid-August and the weaker Tropical Storm Moke. The storm intensified further Monday night, and the family ultimately lost power along with many others on the island.
item.dc:creator: Devin Oldroyd, KSL

item.title: Utah woman returns to New York for 25th anniversary of 9/11
item.description: Salt Lake City's Carrie Pike traveled to New York this week to mark the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks, continuing a relationship she built with families of firefighters killed that day. In the months after 2001, Pike organized a project making more than 400 grief teddy bears for families of firefighters and police officers who died in the attacks, including the 15 members of Manhattan's Engine 54 battalion, which lost every firefighter it sent to the World Trade Center. This year she is delivering 15 American flag blankets donated by Minky Couture to families connected to Engine 54, continuing visits she began at the 20th anniversary in 2021. More than 400 people were expected to gather at Engine 54 alone for Friday's remembrance events.
item.dc:creator: Dan Rascon, KSL

item.title: South Jordan restaurant donates day's sales to Nepal disaster relief fund
item.description: Bawarchi, a South Jordan restaurant, pledged to donate all of one day's sales to Nepal's Prime Minister Disaster Relief Fund as the country recovers from flash floods that have killed more than 1,300 people and a new earthquake that struck this week. Owner Prkash Shah, who has family in Nepal, said the destruction felt "surreal" and that he wanted to do more than his personal donation. Customers including Miranda Westman and Gajushre Stha, who also has family in Nepal, said they were glad to support the relief effort, and the restaurant also planned live music as part of the fundraiser.
item.dc:creator: Debbie Worthen, KSL

item.title: Homeowners ask Logan City to prove right-of-way as project encroaches on property
item.description: Homeowners along Canyon Road in Logan are pushing back on a city trail and pipeline project they say could cut through their yards, after previously losing a fight to save more than a dozen century-old ash trees along the same corridor. Resident Megan Carollo, whose family has owned the property for five generations, delivered a petition signed by about 50 homeowners asking the city to prove its right-of-way claim before proceeding. City spokesman George Woodward said Logan intends to use only 66 of up to 99 feet available along the collector road, but acknowledged an independent contractor's title research to confirm the right-of-way is taking longer than expected.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: Southern Utah man given 15 years in prison for $89M fraud scheme
item.description: Washington City resident Matthew Shane Perkins, 47, was sentenced to 15 years in federal prison for defrauding roughly 200 investors of $89 million by posing as a highly successful day trader. Prosecutors said Perkins ran the scheme through his company Forged Oak LLC in partnership with RentDue Capital, sending investors falsified account statements that inflated fund balances by tens of millions of dollars. He spent the money on luxury vehicles, a plane, a cabin and an $80,000 hunting trip, and pleaded guilty in February to wire fraud after losing or misappropriating nearly all of the funds. He must pay $77.68 million in restitution and will serve three years of probation after his prison term.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: 'Unexpected parenting': Springville mother shares journey of raising adult son with special needs
item.description: Springville nurse Keri Beardall is sharing her experience raising her 32-year-old son Austin, who has lived with intractable epilepsy and developmental delays since infancy, hoping to give voice to parents of adult children with special needs. Beardall, who works in the NICU at Utah Valley Hospital, said Austin's seizures began around four months old and proved resistant to standard medications, eventually revealing lifelong learning and speech delays. After Austin aged out of school services at 22, the family faced new challenges finding support, and it took roughly 15 years for him to receive assistance through the state's Division of Services for People with Disabilities. Beardall said grief remains part of her ongoing journey even as she's grateful for her son.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Utah community helps teen with Down syndrome achieve her dream bear hunt
item.description: A Utah hunting community rallied to help 17-year-old Izzy Jackson of the Uinta Basin, who has Down syndrome, go on a black bear hunt after years of running a lemonade stand to benefit a local food bank caught a hunter's attention. That hunter donated his own bear tag and offered to mentor Izzy, with additional support from the Utah Conservation Officers Association, local houndsmen and family. After hounds treed a bear, the group worked together to get Izzy safely to the site for her hunt, a story organizers describe as showing how community generosity comes full circle.
item.dc:creator: Adam Eakle, KSL

item.title: Highland teen makes history as Miss America's Teen 2027
item.description: Highland teenager Elle Anderson, competing as Miss Utah's Teen, was crowned Miss America's Teen 2027 on Saturday, becoming the first Utahn to win the national teen title. Anderson beat out finalists from Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas and Minnesota, edging first runner-up Madalyn Sullivan of Mississippi, and earned a $40,000 scholarship on top of the $8,000 she won for her state title in May. Anderson has used her platform to promote CPR training and heart-health awareness through a partnership with the American Heart Association, a cause rooted in the death of her infant brother Stone from a cardiac event. She said she has trained hundreds of Utah teens in CPR and hopes to expand the effort nationally during her year of service.
item.dc:creator: Annette Campbell, KSL

item.title: He was nervous to call 988. What happened when he picked up the phone?
item.description: Utahn Jordan Starks, now three years sober, credits the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline with helping him through mental health struggles tied to addiction and his gender transition, despite initial fear about what calling would be like. Starks said crisis workers at Utah's Huntsman Mental Health Institute, which handles 988 calls in the state, simply listened and stayed with him through difficult moments without judgment. Utah's 988 system fielded more than 130,000 calls last fiscal year, a 14% increase, and Dr. Eric Monson of the University of Utah's Zero Suicide Program said the line is meant to support callers rather than automatically send them to a hospital.
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: Provo amends outdoor lighting code for dark sky requirements
item.description: The Provo City Council unanimously approved an ordinance requiring new developments to use dark-sky-compliant outdoor lighting, joining other Utah communities working to reduce light pollution. The new standards, based on principles from the Illuminating Engineering Society and DarkSky International, require lower color-temperature bulbs, fully shielded fixtures directing light downward, and capped display brightness, applying to new installations and major remodels rather than retroactively. Provo Power director Patricio Hernandez said the utility has already been installing dark-sky-compliant streetlights in recent years, and the council said it plans to revisit the rules to address holiday and event lighting.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Second man charged in violent 2025 West Valley burglary and assault
item.description: Prosecutors charged a second man, 32-year-old Pedro Isaac Bonilla Urbina, in a March 2025 home invasion in which two men broke into a West Valley City apartment, robbed a woman of jewelry and bank cards, and sexually assaulted her at gunpoint while her young daughter was in another room. Bonilla Urbina faces aggravated robbery, aggravated burglary, two counts of aggravated sexual assault and related charges; the first man charged, Efrain Jose Gregorio Monroy-Lara, was identified last year through the victim's stolen bank cards and a national DNA database. Prosecutors described the case in charging documents as "something out of the movies," noting the victim begged for her life and for her daughter's safety during the assault. Monroy-Lara's next court hearing is scheduled for Sept. 14.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Fire breaks out at Salt Lake City recycling center for second time in 4 months
item.description: A fire broke out at a Poplar Grove neighborhood recycling facility on Orange Street in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, the second blaze at the same METech Recycling building in four months after a May 19 fire. Salt Lake City Fire Capt. Chad Jepperson said the single-alarm fire quickly escalated to a second alarm requiring about 50 firefighters, and a small grass fire sparked by embers nearby was also extinguished. No injuries were reported and all employees evacuated safely; the building's concrete exterior kept flames from spreading inside, though officials urged nearby residents to stay indoors and close windows because of smoke from burning wood, cardboard and electronic waste. The cause remains under investigation.
item.dc:creator: Mary Culbertson and Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: He's a 'horrible, horrible human being,' mother calls her daughter's killer
item.description: Tammy Edmunds testified before the Utah Board of Pardons and Parole on Tuesday urging that Anthony Jeffrey Christensen, convicted of murdering her daughter Kammy Mae Edmunds in 2020, never be released from prison. Christensen, now 44, beat his fiancee to death in 2017 and tried to stage the killing as a drunk-driving accident, but a medical examiner found her injuries were blunt-force trauma inconsistent with a car crash. Because Christensen's scheduled parole hearing isn't until 2040, the family requested an earlier impact hearing out of concern Tammy Edmunds might not be alive by then. She described her daughter as kind and universally loved but said Christensen was "a horrible, horrible human being."
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Labor Day DUI enforcement highlights efforts to prevent impaired driving in Utah
item.description: Utah Highway Patrol and dozens of local agencies ramped up DUI patrols over Labor Day weekend as the state closed out its "100 Deadliest Days" stretch, with more than 245 extra overtime DUI shifts logged across 39 agencies statewide, per the Department of Public Safety. UHP Lt. Zach Randall said troopers suspect impairment and speeding contributed to a fatal Salt Lake County crash over the weekend and stressed that drunk driving is entirely preventable. State Rep. Steve Eliason said he's preparing legislation for the next session that would expand alcohol-purchase restrictions to more DUI offenders and could penalize bars with high rates of DUI-linked patrons, citing more than 100 annual Utah drunk-driving deaths. Randall urged drivers to arrange a sober ride before they start drinking, noting enforcement remained heightened into Monday night as the holiday wrapped up.
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: Utahns flock to Millcreek Canyon for affordable Labor Day getaway
item.description: Cooler temperatures drew hikers, mountain bikers and picnicking families to Millcreek Canyon on Labor Day for one of the last big outdoor outings of the summer. Mountain biker Alex Khajavi said the canyon offered inexpensive recreation after a tough, hot riding season at its lower elevation. The Warnick family grilled steaks and corn at a canyon picnic site, with Brock Warnick saying Utah's outdoor access is hard to match for the price elsewhere. Parking filled quickly as crowds took advantage of the unofficial end of summer, even though the season doesn't officially end until the autumnal equinox on Sept. 22.
item.dc:creator: Annette Campbell, KSL

item.title: Salt Lake unveils markers noting 1866 lynching and a historic alternative gathering spot
item.description: Salt Lake City unveiled two new historical markers on Aug. 25 as part of a pilot program, led by Councilman Chris Wharton, meant to broaden the range of stories commemorated around the city beyond pioneer-era history. One marker, sought by the Sema Hadithi African American Heritage and Culture Foundation, memorializes Thomas Coleman, a Black man lynched in Salt Lake City in 1866 near where his body was found. The other, pursued by the Mildred Berryman Institute for LGBTIQ2S+ Utah History, honors the Sun Tavern, a bar that served as a de facto community hub for gay, lesbian and bisexual Utahns after it opened in 1973. Wharton said the $30,000 initiative funded only these two markers for now, but he hopes to secure more funding to add additional stories in the future.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: 'Moderate to severe' turbulence reported prior to fatal plane crash in Utah Lake
item.description: A newly released NTSB preliminary report found that multiple aircraft near Provo Municipal Airport reported moderate to severe turbulence shortly before an ATP Flight School training plane crashed into Utah Lake on Aug. 7, killing student pilot Chase Riley Day, 25, and seriously injuring his flight instructor. The Cessna 172 Skyhawk entered a rapid descent seconds after takeoff, and airport security cameras captured dust plumes moving through the area beforehand. The plane's cabin, engine and both wings were found submerged in Provo Bay within a roughly 100-foot debris field. The NTSB says its investigation into the crash's cause is continuing; Day was laid to rest on Aug. 15.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Provo mayor defends Vesper Amphitheater as Vivint founder, others express concerns
item.description: Provo Mayor Marsha Judkins urged residents to let the review process play out for the proposed 20,000-seat Vesper Amphitheater in Provo Canyon, an Osmond-family-backed project that also includes a 75-room hotel and extensive parking on land partly owned by the city. Developers recently withdrew their application to rework plans addressing concerns about traffic, noise and parking, and plan to resubmit by month's end. Vivint founder Todd Pedersen, an Orem resident near the canyon mouth, said he isn't opposed to development generally but is alarmed by the potential traffic impact, and the city of Orem has formally objected that the project's impacts are too significant to ignore. Judkins said she isn't committed to approval "at all costs" but believes exploring the proposal is the responsible course.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Waves of layoffs are sweeping across Utah. Here's what workers losing their jobs should know
item.description: Thousands of Utah workers have lost jobs in 2026 amid cutbacks at companies including Tyson Foods, Qualtrics, Crumbl and Sheraton, with Tyson laying off more than 700 employees at its Eagle Mountain plant as it shutters facilities amid a 75-year low in U.S. cattle supplies. Laid-off maintenance worker Austin Campbell said he's grateful for his degree but wary of relocating to another Tyson site given the industry's turmoil, and noted the company's above-market pay makes finding comparable wages elsewhere difficult. Nationally, job cuts are running 41% below last year's pace, the lowest January-through-August total since 2022, but hiring has also slowed to a "no hire, no fire" dynamic, according to Challenger, Gray & Christmas. The Utah Department of Workforce Services said it offers free assistance, including job-search help, for displaced workers navigating the transition.
item.dc:creator: Art Raymond, Deseret News

item.title: Competency evaluation ordered for man accused of setting Timp Fire
item.description: A 4th District Court judge ordered a mental competency evaluation for Conrad Jared Larsen, 46, who is charged with four counts of arson including the July 9 Timp Fire that forced evacuations near Timpooneke Campground. Larsen's defense attorney argued in her petition that he struggles to understand the charges against him, can't recall key details of the fires or conversations with counsel, and has described a "supernatural force" and hearing spirits he called "cursed." A letter from Larsen's brother cited a self-reported diagnosis of schizoid personality disorder and described him as estranged from family with rigid, altered thinking, though the brother said he doesn't view Larsen as malicious or violent. The Utah Department of Human Services has been ordered to arrange a forensic evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Crowds flock to Utah canyon areas to mark Labor Day
item.description: Hundreds of people packed Tibble Fork Reservoir in American Fork Canyon on Labor Day to paddleboard, swim and relax in mild, sunny weather. Visitors including Sabrina Longman and Kiersty Sutton, the latter visiting from Idaho with a group of students, praised the reservoir's scenery and atmosphere. South Jordan resident Chris Keller, who brought his family after a morning of four-wheeling and hiking, said the outing was a fun way to mark the end of summer before kids return to school. Several visitors expressed mixed feelings about summer ending, with some looking forward to Utah's fall colors.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: This Salt Lake City taco shop is looking to expand without losing unique 'alley street feel'
item.description: Five years after opening in a Salt Lake City alley, ROCTACO is looking to expand its globally inspired taco concept to more locations in Utah and potentially beyond, co-owner Rick Timmons told KSL. Timmons and his brother Ryan drew the menu's international flavors, including Korean bulgogi and Indian chicken tikka masala tacos, from their Church of Jesus Christ mission trips and Rick's two decades living in Asia, while resisting the "fusion" label. The brothers brought in culinary experts for each cuisine to ensure authenticity and spent a year and a half perfecting their made-from-scratch tortillas. Rick Timmons said the concept has proven itself enough to justify moving from a single location toward broader growth.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: 1 killed in crash on state Route 89 in Utah County
item.description: A passenger died Monday morning after a Honda Civic crossed double yellow lines to pass another vehicle near Birdseye and struck a southbound Toyota Tacoma head-on, according to the Utah Highway Patrol. The crash occurred around 10:30 a.m. on state Route 89, and both drivers were taken to nearby hospitals by ambulance. Authorities had not released additional details about the deceased passenger's identity as of the report.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: 'Remarkable' noses — new dogs in Utah corrections program can search for electronics
item.description: Utah's Adult Probation and Parole introduced two new K-9s, Glitch and Cypher, trained to sniff out phones, SD cards and other electronic storage devices hidden by people on probation or parole, particularly the roughly 1,700 sex offenders under internet-access restrictions among the more than 15,000 people the agency supervises. Officer Josh Paxman said Glitch found two hidden phones in 20 minutes at a home where other agents had searched unsuccessfully for 90 minutes. The dogs, donated by the nonprofit Defenders for Children, were trained in Indianapolis and have searched roughly 80 Utah residences combined since arriving, recovering phones, a drone and multiple smartwatches. Defenders for Children executive director Toni Clark said the dogs serve as a reminder to offenders that violations will send them back to prison.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Peteetneet Fire in Payson now 60% contained
item.description: The Peteetneet Fire burning near Nebo Loop Road in Payson reached 60% containment after crews worked through the night to secure its perimeter, according to Utah Division of Forestry, Fire and State Lands spokesperson Kayli Guild. The blaze, which grew to about 45 acres after starting Sunday, is being fought by both ground crews and aircraft, with no closures currently in place. Guild said a golf course separates the fire from nearby neighborhoods and that there have been no impacts to infrastructure or watersheds so far, though officials asked people to avoid the area. The fire's cause is confirmed as human-caused but remains under investigation.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: Driver killed early Sunday in rollover crash
item.description: A driver was killed early Sunday when a BMW went off westbound I-80 near 6200 West in Salt Lake City for unknown reasons and rolled down an embankment, according to the Utah Highway Patrol. Cashton Gamble, 19, of Heber City, was partially ejected and pronounced dead at the scene; a 21-year-old passenger was hospitalized in critical condition with multiple broken bones and head injuries. Neither occupant was wearing a seatbelt, and investigators are looking at speed and impairment as possible contributing factors.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Bicyclist hit, killed in Provo
item.description: A 63-year-old cyclist died after being struck by a vehicle exiting I-15 at the University Avenue off-ramp and Lakeview Parkway in Provo on Monday morning, police said. He was taken to Utah Valley Hospital but did not survive his injuries. Provo police said the driver is cooperating with the investigation and that impairment is not suspected, and the intersection reopened around midday.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Company believes drone cloud seeding tech could help restore the Great Salt Lake in the future
item.description: California-based Rainmaker Technology Corporation says its drone-based cloud seeding process produced 19 million gallons of precipitation over three hours in a recent Alaska test, and founder Augustus Doricko told KSL the company is partnering with the Utah Department of Natural Resources on plans to eventually apply the technology to help restore the shrinking Great Salt Lake. Doricko said Rainmaker uses radar, balloons, drones and satellites to identify clouds holding supercooled water droplets, then seeds them with dust so they grow into precipitation-sized flakes. Utah Division of Water Resources meteorologist Jonathan Jennings said the Alaska test built on 2017's SNOWIE research and that verified precipitation gains, even modest ones, could meaningfully ease stress on Utah's water supply over a decade or two. Doricko acknowledged critics' concerns about cumulative effects of cloud-seeding chemicals and said stronger federal regulation will likely be needed as the technology scales.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: Holocaust survivor to speak at University of Utah
item.description: Sora Vigorito, the youngest known survivor of Nazi doctor Josef Mengele's twin experiments at Auschwitz, will speak at the University of Utah on Sept. 15, according to Rabbi Moshe Nigri of Chabad on Campus. Vigorito was 3 years old when she and her twin sister were taken to Auschwitz in 1944; her sister died in the camp, but Vigorito survived until its 1945 liberation. Nigri said Vigorito rarely travels to Utah given the state's small Jewish population, and organizers expect 150 to 200 attendees at the 7 p.m. event in the Gardner Commons' Siciliano Auditorium, co-sponsored by several campus interfaith groups. Nigri said the story carries a message relevant to people of any faith.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: From the beginning of the Edwards Era, Dave Hanna watched a leadership guru at work
item.description: Dave Hanna, who worked in BYU's sports information office as LaVell Edwards began his head coaching tenure in 1972, has written a new book, "LaVell's Leadership Playbook," drawing business leadership lessons from Edwards' coaching style. Hanna recalled Edwards being overcome with emotion after BYU's 1974 upset of 16th-ranked Arizona State, and said the moment reflected how deeply players respected Edwards' leadership. After a career at Procter & Gamble and as a corporate consultant, Hanna said he came to view Edwards as the equal of top business executives he'd studied, prompting him to identify eight leadership principles Edwards consistently applied. Hanna's book arrives the same month as a second book on Edwards, "The Leadership of LaVell Edwards" by Mark D. Ogletree and Dave McCann, underscoring the coach's enduring legacy a decade after his death.
item.dc:creator: Lee Benson, Deseret News

item.title: Utah data centers promise jobs and revenue, but opponents say benefits disappear
item.description: Utah residents and researchers are questioning whether promised economic benefits of new data centers, including lower electricity and property tax bills, actually materialize, according to reporting centered on Box Elder County activist Brenna Williams' opposition to the proposed Stratos data center. USC professor Shon Hiatt told a legislative interim committee that investor-owned utilities like Rocky Mountain Power haven't passed data-center costs to other customers so far, but warned that trend could change as larger facilities arrive, and that utilities without similar resources tend to raise rates instead. University of Utah public finance researcher Maddy Oritt described a "boomerang effect" in property taxes, where new data-center construction initially lowers other residents' rates by expanding the tax base, but the effect fades as the facilities' taxable equipment depreciates over time. The story notes Utah's Truth in Taxation system separates real property like buildings from personal property like servers, which is taxed differently as it ages.
item.dc:creator: Leah Bowers, Deseret News

item.title: Wildfire threatens structures in Payson
item.description: The Peteetneet Fire, burning near Nebo Loop Road in Payson, grew to roughly 45 acres and was threatening nearby structures as of Sunday night, when it was 0% contained, according to Utah Fire Info. Firefighters battled the blaze from the air and ground, with a golf course roughly half a mile wide serving as a buffer between the fire and nearby homes, Payson Fire Department spokesperson Scott Spencer said. Utah Fire Info asked residents to avoid the area to give firefighters room to work safely.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: Pineview draw down brings rare low levels, slump in activity
item.description: Crowds at Pineview Reservoir near Huntsville were unusually thin heading into Labor Day weekend as Ogden City crews draw down the lake to replace a 1970s-era 36-inch water pipeline serving about 120,000 people. Water levels have fallen to roughly 17% of normal and are expected to dip to near 2% of normal, or about 2,000 acre-feet, by mid-September, the lowest since the original pipeline was installed, according to the Weber Basin Water Conservancy District. Anglers Sam Fortney and Kameron Mickelson, the latter having driven from Mesquite, Nevada, in hopes of catching tiger muskies concentrated in the shrinking lake, both remarked on how strange the low water looked. Club Rec co-owner Paul Avner said business has slowed at the reservoir's Cemetery Point location, which will move to reservations-only after Labor Day, while the company's Willard Bay site remains busy.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: 22-year-old Kaysville woman with Down syndrome becomes certified fitness instructor
item.description: Aubry Alldredge, 22, of Kaysville became the first person with Down syndrome to earn certification as a UpBeat Barre instructor at VASA Fitness after years of attending classes there. She recently taught her first class to more than 60 people and says she loves motivating others and helping everyone feel included. Co-owner and instructor Jane Johnson praised Alldredge's quick grasp of choreography and stage presence, and said the gym hopes to bring her on as an official instructor. Alldredge also co-wrote a children's book with her sisters, called "I Have a Six Pack," inspired by the six rescue dogs she cares for, meant to promote inclusion for people with Down syndrome.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Spanish Fork woman to serve year in prison for cyberstalking, harassing 2 victims
item.description: A federal judge sentenced Kailin Wang, 43, of Spanish Fork to a year in prison and three years of probation after she pleaded guilty to cyberstalking two men she met on dating sites in California starting in 2017 and 2018. Prosecutors said Wang waged years-long harassment campaigns against the men and their families, including defamatory online posts, false reports to law enforcement and the FBI's internet crimes unit, and threats against one victim. She also pleaded guilty in Utah state court to a false statement and forgery charge for using misleading evidence to seek a protective order against one of the men. Prosecutors noted Wang had a prior 2013 stalking conviction in New York, and her probation now bars her from contacting the victims or their families and requires her to disclose the conviction to future partners.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: 'Trackflation' is here: Why Utah's young runners are getting so fast
item.description: KSL profiled the rise of unusually fast youth running times in Utah, a trend coaches call "trackflation," centered on 13-year-old Provo runner Angelina Alder, whose 4:38.25 mile this summer set an age-group world record. Roadrunner Junior Club founder John Hedengren, a former BYU All-American runner who now teaches chemical engineering, said times that were nationally elite a generation ago no longer crack the top 100. He attributed the shift to wider access to elite training knowledge, better nutrition and coaching, "super shoes" with carbon plates that measurably improve running efficiency for some athletes, and Utah County's altitude, which can boost endurance at lower elevations. Hedengren's club has grown from 17 athletes in 2019 to more than 180 today, and he said watching peers like Alder succeed inspires other young runners to push their own limits.
item.dc:creator: Eric Cabrera, KSL

item.title: $1.2M donation to UNICEF from Church of Jesus Christ to care for moms, babies in Pakistan
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints announced a two-year, $1.2 million collaboration with UNICEF to improve maternal and newborn care for about 410,000 mothers in Pakistan, part of a broader initiative aimed at 1.5 million mothers across South Asia. Relief Society General President Camille N. Johnson said the effort aims to close care gaps around childbirth, while UNICEF officials Pernille Ironside and Sanjay Wijesekera said the funding will help prevent some of the roughly 700 newborn deaths and two maternal deaths Pakistan sees each day. Elder Kelly R. Johnson, the church's Asia Area president, said the goal is to extend life-saving care to more mothers and infants in the region. The funding will go toward supplies, health-worker training and improved data systems to help identify high-risk pregnancies.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Developers 'hit pause' on Vesper Amphitheater plans after public pushback
item.description: Developers behind the Osmond family's proposed 20,000-seat Vesper Amphitheater in Provo Canyon withdrew their application to Provo City after strong public opposition, including a formal letter of concern this week from neighboring Orem over noise, traffic and impacts on Mount Timpanogos Park. Vesper representative Bryan Bayles told KSL developers plan to resubmit a revised application by month's end that shrinks retail and restaurant space to 40,000 square feet while keeping the venue's 20,000-seat capacity and a planned 75-room hotel. Orem officials, including council member Crystal Muhlestein, remain skeptical any revision can resolve concerns about commercializing the canyon, while Provo council member Travis Hoban said he remains undecided after touring the site. Executive director David Osmond said the developers are Utah natives who understand the area's sensitivity and are working to address public feedback.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Advice for Utah homebuyers as rates near previous highs
item.description: A global sell-off in government bonds this week pushed U.S. mortgage rates toward 7% for the first time since January 2025, with Freddie Mac's 30-year fixed average climbing to 6.71% and some lenders quoting even higher. Economists including First American's Mark Fleming and reporting from The Wall Street Journal linked the rise to 10-year Treasury yields hitting a three-year high amid concerns over the ongoing U.S.-Israel war against Iran and a national debt topping $40 trillion. Zions Bank Mortgage's Jeremy Holmgren said the psychological impact of a 7% rate outweighs its practical difference from 6.75%, and urged buyers to focus on today's affordability rather than trying to time the market. He added that buyers who don't wait on the sidelines may benefit from less competition and more leverage with sellers as Utah's housing inventory continues to grow.
item.dc:creator: Lisa Riley Roche, Deseret News

item.title: Moroni Elementary educator Talia Casares named Utah's 2027 'Teacher of the Year'
item.description: Utah's State Board of Education named Talia Casares, a sixth-grade Spanish dual-language immersion teacher at Moroni Elementary in the North Sanpete School District, as the state's 2027 Teacher of the Year. Casares, originally from Mexico City and a BYU master's graduate who researched literacy and STEM integration in dual-language classrooms, was chosen from five finalists by a committee of state board, advocacy, higher-education and charter-school representatives. She has taught for nine years and previously won the 2025 Utah Coalition for Educational Technology's Innovative Teacher Award. Casares receives $10,000 and will represent Utah in a national teacher-of-the-year competition next year, while the four other finalists each received $2,000.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: How one woman's grief turned into a yearslong mission to prevent suicide
item.description: Salt Lake County tax lien coordinator Ray Lancaster, whose adult son died by suicide in 2017, spent eight years pushing the county to formally recognize September as Suicide Prevention and Awareness Month, finally succeeding this week with help from County Treasurer Sheila Srivastava, whose teenage son survived a mental health crisis after witnessing his father's fatal heart attack. Mayor Jenny Wilson and the County Council signed a proclamation Tuesday urging residents to learn warning signs, check on struggling loved ones, and share the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, while inviting the public to Saturday's Out of the Darkness Community Walk in West Jordan. Wilson grew emotional recounting the recent death of Colin Hilton, the former Utah Olympic Legacy Foundation president. Lancaster and Srivastava said sharing their stories has helped them find community, and both plan to keep advocating for awareness beyond this year's proclamation.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Utah mother of young twins accused by federal grand jury of abuse
item.description: A federal grand jury indicted Fayette Whitehorse, 27, of Aneth on two counts of aggravated child abuse in Indian country after her 3-month-old twins were airlifted from Blanding to Primary Children's Hospital on Aug. 24 with multiple fractures and, in the boy's case, a brain hemorrhage. Whitehorse was arrested Aug. 26 following an FBI interview in which, according to charging documents, she admitted causing several of the injuries out of frustration while caring for the infants. The twins, born prematurely in May, had fractures in different stages of healing, indicating repeated incidents over time. The case remains pending in federal court following the indictment.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Historic Dixie Sunbowl gets major upgrades, increases capacity
item.description: St. George's nearly 80-year-old Dixie Sunbowl stadium completed a roughly $3.7 million renovation, funded by a voter-approved bond and Washington County RAP tax funds, that replaced its aging concrete bleachers and boosted capacity by about 1,000 seats to 7,300. Contractor Gene Madsen of Hughes General Contractors said crews demolished and rebuilt the venue in about a year after last year's rodeo to address safety and comfort issues the deteriorating 1947 stadium could no longer support. Madsen said the venue, originally built through community donations and Lions Club labor, remains deeply meaningful to St. George residents. The Sunbowl holds its grand reopening Sept. 10, just ahead of the Dixie Round-up Rodeo running Sept. 17-19.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Fire in Washington County burns multiple homes
item.description: A fire broke out Friday afternoon near Wagon Wheel Drive and Cottonmill East Avenue in Washington City, sending black smoke over the community and destroying or damaging multiple homes and vehicles.
