Battalion Chief Brandon Moore said the blaze started in one building before spreading to a shed used to store live ammunition, which ignited and forced crews to briefly retreat for safety before two more structures caught fire amid windy conditions. Neighbor Lani Lawrence, whose own home burned down in 2013, said she feared history was repeating when she saw the smoke while driving home from a grocery store. Fire crews expected the response to stretch for hours as they worked to fully extinguish the blaze.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Afro Utah Festival returns, highlighting the mix of cultures in Utah rooted in Africa
item.description: The Afro Utah Festival returns for its sixth year Saturday to Salt Lake City's Main Library plaza, offering free food, entertainment, crafts and business booths celebrating Afro Caribbean, African American, Afro Latino and African cultures. Organizer Gloria Mensah of the GK Folks Foundation, originally from Nigeria, said the event began in 2021 to support Black-owned businesses hurt by the pandemic and has since grown to draw upward of 5,000 attendees. This year's festival runs noon to 9 p.m. and is headlined by Virgin Islands soca artist Pumpa, with a stretch of 200 East closing for the event. A companion Afro Utah Awards ceremony Friday recognized community members for their achievements ahead of Saturday's festivities.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: 10 food deals to check out this Labor Day weekend
item.description: Deseret News rounded up Labor Day weekend food deals from national chains, including discounted snacks at 7-Eleven and Speedway, bonus gift-card offers at The Cheesecake Factory, and a buy-one-get-one sub deal at Firehouse Subs. Other highlighted offers include $4.99 large one-topping pizzas at Little Caesars, a buy-one-get-one sandwich deal at Jimmy John's, a discounted dozen doughnuts at Krispy Kreme, and Grubhub promotions like free delivery on orders over $50, with most deals running through the holiday weekend. Cracker Barrel is offering a collectible toy or store discount with kids' meal purchases, and Olive Garden's Never-Ending Pasta Bowl returns through late November. The roundup notes shoppers should check each chain's loyalty app for exact redemption terms.
item.dc:creator: Caitlin Keith, Deseret News

item.title: Utah pauses age verification rule enforcement with Pornhub owner pending court ruling
item.description: Utah's Division of Consumer Protection agreed to pause enforcement of a proposed adult-website age-verification rule against Aylo Freesites, the owner of Pornhub and RedTube, while a federal judge weighs the company's request to block the state's underlying law. In exchange, Aylo agreed to keep geofencing its sites to block Utah users for the duration of the stipulation, which lasts until the rule takes effect or U.S. District Judge David Barlow rules on the injunction request. The dispute traces back to an earlier Utah law requiring adult sites to verify users' ages, which led Pornhub to block Utah traffic entirely, and a stronger 2026 law adding enforcement authority and targeting VPN workarounds. Aylo sued in April arguing there is no reliable way to verify a user's true location, and Judge Barlow heard arguments on the injunction request in July without yet ruling; the agreement does not affect enforcement against other adult sites.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: 9 officers cleared by DA for 2025 standoff ending in fatal shooting
item.description: Salt Lake County District Attorney Sim Gill announced Friday that nine law enforcement officers were legally justified in using deadly force during a September 2025 standoff that ended in the fatal shooting of Elhelbawy Adam Idrees, 26. According to Gill's final report, officers from the West Jordan Police Department and the State Bureau of Investigation responded after a 911 caller said Idrees was inside a house threatening him with a "machine gun," and later learned Idrees was wanted on an outstanding warrant and had been flagged as armed and dangerous. After hours of failed negotiation, officers deployed gas to force Idrees outside; when he emerged holding a rifle and appeared to raise it toward officers, nine members of a joint SWAT team opened fire, contributing to the 81 rounds investigators recovered at the scene. Officer Alex Hofheins told investigators he believed Idrees posed an immediate threat to officers and nearby residents. Idrees was declared dead at the scene.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: New affordable housing development breaks ground in Salt Lake City
item.description: City leaders and developers broke ground Thursday in Salt Lake City on Camden Court, a new 96-unit income-restricted apartment project meant to help working families remain in the city amid rising housing costs. Officials said the development targets households earning between 30% and 60% of area median income, noting that nearly half of Salt Lake City renters are considered cost-burdened. Charles Schmid of developer Chelsea Investment Corporation said the project is about more than unit counts, while Utah representative Jon Olsen said federal, state and local funding will keep rents affordable, with one-bedroom units starting around $600 a month. Mayor Erin Mendenhall said the project builds on recent neighborhood improvements along 300 West, including protected bike lanes. Construction is expected to take about 20 months, with Camden Court slated to open in spring 2028.
item.dc:creator: Annette Campbell, KSL

item.title: Cornbelly's opens Dolly Parton-themed corn maze in Spanish Fork
item.description: Cornbelly's Adventure Park in Spanish Fork opened its fall season Friday with a corn maze designed as a tribute to Dolly Parton, a three-years-in-the-making project that took on added poignancy after the singer's death just over a week after the design was announced. Marketing and events director Kamille Combs said Parton was a natural fit given her ties to farming, family and community, and the attraction will play her music and offer Dolly-themed trivia throughout the maze. On Sept. 25, timed to reference her song "9 to 5," Cornbelly's will host a fundraising storytime event benefiting Dolly Parton's Imagination Library literacy program. Co-founder Brett Herbst said the attraction is meant to help families reconnect with Utah's agricultural roots as urban growth consumes farmland along the Wasatch Front. This year's Cornbelly's also includes sunflower fields, tractor rides, apple cannons and a new "Digging Zone."
item.dc:creator: Brenna Donnelly, KSL

item.title: 'Huge milestone': U. opens Native Ascent House, residential facility for Indigenous students
item.description: The University of Utah cut the ribbon Thursday on Native Ascent House, a new residential facility on Officer's Circle built to support Indigenous students, currently housing 11 students including sophomore Cliftene Duncan, a Northern Ute from Fort Duchesne. The house operates under the university's Native Ascent Scholars Program and its Center for Native Excellence and Tribal Engagement, a four-year effort meant to foster community and academic success among Native students. Student Tavamawisi Groves, a Ute tribal member, said the shared living space reinforces cultural bonds and lets students combine their heritage with their education. The program continues despite Utah's HB261, a 2024 law restricting identity-based programming at state universities, because of a carve-out tied to the university's agreement with the Ute Indian Tribe and tribes' distinct status as sovereign nations. Program manager Tashina Barber and student affairs vice president Lori McDonald both called the opening a major milestone for building community among Native students on campus.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Park City dentist accused of supplying drugs to teen girl
item.description: Provo dentist Benjamin James Wilson, 49, who practices in Park City, was charged Thursday in Summit County's 3rd District Court with drug distribution and related counts after a 16-year-old girl told investigators he supplied her with drugs and alcohol. Charging documents state the girl traveled to Park City with Wilson in June, where he allegedly gave her MDMA, marijuana and psilocybin mushrooms, plus alcohol, and later gave her nitrous oxide at his dental office. Prosecutors also allege Wilson had the girl touch him inappropriately in exchange for additional drugs. Wilson faces two second-degree felony drug distribution counts along with misdemeanor charges for unlawful sexual conduct with a minor, providing alcohol to a minor, and contributing to the delinquency of a minor.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: New Intermountain Health clinic supports families navigating pregnancy after loss
item.description: Intermountain Health opened a Pregnancy After Loss Clinic in July at Intermountain Medical Center in Murray, one of only nine such certified programs in the country, to support parents who are pregnant again after losing a child. Senior practice manager Lizbeth Hernandez, who lost a daughter to Sudden Infant Death Syndrome and later became pregnant again, said the clinic grew partly out of her own experience with the anxiety that follows a loss. Beyond standard prenatal care, the program provides tailored emotional support for patients and trains caregivers to recognize how a prior loss can shape a patient's experience during a new pregnancy. Hernandez said the goal is for patients and families to feel supported while giving caregivers the tools to navigate difficult conversations. Patients need a referral from their provider to access the clinic.
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: 'They need help': Utah restaurateur from Nepal holding fundraiser to aid flood-ravaged nation
item.description: South Jordan restaurant owners Biplove Timilsina and his wife, Navita Poudyal, both originally from Nepal, are holding a fundraiser Tuesday at their restaurant, Bawarchi Indian Cuisine, to help victims of flooding in Nepal that has killed at least 1,200 people and left about 4,000 missing. Proceeds from that day's sales and any additional donations will go to the Nepal Prime Minister's Disaster Relief Fund, managed by the Nepalese government. Timilsina, who operates several Utah restaurants including Big Daddy's Pizza and has lived in the U.S. since 1997, said he still visits Nepal regularly and estimated the fundraiser could raise around $10,000. He compared the scale of destruction to Nepal's 2015 earthquake, saying entire villages and cities were wiped out by the flooding. A Nepalese band will perform at the event, and Poudyal said the community felt compelled to act given how many families are suffering.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Fans optimistic as Utah opens 2026 college football season
item.description: Utah Utes fans at Rice-Eccles Stadium expressed optimism about the 2026 season as the team built a 31-7 halftime lead over Idaho in Thursday's season opener. Fans interviewed by KSL, including freshman Jared Bourne and Jacob Timpson, praised the team's performance and the stadium atmosphere despite the Utes fielding a new head coach, Morgan Scalley, this year. Fan Summer Duffin said the game-day environment at Rice-Eccles was unmatched, crediting the crowd's energy. Several fans said they were eager for the season ahead and confident about Utah's chances.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: Utahn with history of dismissed child sex charges pleads guilty in federal court
item.description: Jonathan Jareth Soberanis, 31, pleaded guilty Thursday in federal court to distribution and transportation of child sexual abuse material, ending years of state cases in which he was repeatedly charged with sex crimes against children only to be found mentally incompetent and released. Stephanie Davis, mother of one of his alleged victims, said Soberanis showed up at her Lehi home in January 2022 attempting to reach her 7-year-old child, months after she had flagged him to her husband from a separate case involving a child at a Lehi recreation center. Federal prosecutors said Soberanis used social media, the dark web and encrypted cloud storage to host illicit material, and forensic evaluators diagnosed him over the years with conditions including fetal alcohol spectrum disorder and autism amid a contested, years-long competency battle before U.S. District Judge David Barlow. Soberanis told the court in his plea statement that he knowingly received, kept and distributed child pornography and chose to plead guilty without an agreement. Davis said prosecutors have indicated they intend to seek reopening of the previously dismissed state charges against him.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: UVU fights food insecurity with free cooking classes
item.description: Utah Valley University is offering free Budget Cooking Classes on Fridays that teach students basic cooking skills using ingredients from the school's student food pantry and its student-run Grit Garden. University spokesperson Sharon Turner said the classes respond to rising food costs and survey data showing nearly half of Utah students report some level of food insecurity, with a 2018 UVU-specific survey finding 51% of respondents had gone hungry because they couldn't afford food. Turner said UVU distributed more than 67,000 pounds of pantry food and 16,000 pounds of garden produce to students last year. The classes are open to any student and are meant to help those living independently for the first time learn to cook with what they have on hand.
item.dc:creator: Bryanna Willis, KSL

item.title: Man who allegedly couldn't wait 'to kill a gay person' charged with hate crime
item.description: An 18-year-old Provo man, Damyen Vainuku, was charged Thursday in 3rd District Court with stalking and weapons offenses carrying hate-crime "targeting" enhancements after prosecutors said he threatened to kill a former West High School classmate because of the victim's sexual orientation. Charging documents say Salt Lake City police began investigating in August after a SafeUT tip reported threats to shoot the victim and his family, and that a search of Vainuku's electronics turned up firearm photos and messages including a vow to kill a gay person. Police say they identified 13 specific threats of violence involving a firearm and that Vainuku also threatened to distribute intimate videos of the victim. Salt Lake County District Attorney Sim Gill condemned the threats as making the community less safe and said his office's victim services team will support the victim and his family.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: State park managers urge safety ahead of Labor Day weekend
item.description: With Jordanelle Reservoir still calm but expected to fill for Labor Day weekend, Utah state park officials and boaters urged caution ahead of the holiday crowds. Boater Chris Stuber said many people don't know rules like the mandatory Coast Guard-approved life jackets or the 150-foot wakeless zone, which he called a common cause of accidents. Jordanelle State Park manager Amanda White urged visitors to check the forecast, be patient and use the park's free lifejacket loaner stations, noting the reservoir typically hits boat capacity by midmorning on the holiday's busiest day. White advised boaters facing crowds at the main Hailstone ramp to consider launching instead from Ross Creek or Rock Cliff.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: 1 dead after boat overturns, sinks at Echo Reservoir
item.description: One person died and three others, including a child, were hospitalized after a fishing boat overturned and sank at Echo Reservoir in Coalville, according to the Summit County Sheriff's Office. Witnesses spotted the sinking boat and four people in the water around 11:30 a.m. and pulled all four to shore, but one victim died at the scene. The conditions of the three hospitalized survivors have not been released, and investigators are still working to determine what caused the boat to overturn.
item.dc:creator: Devin Oldroyd, KSL

item.title: 60-minute delays possible in Utah during Labor Day weekend despite record-high gas prices
item.description: AAA reported that gas prices are on track to set a Labor Day record this year, with Utah's average of $4.42 per gallon running 28 cents above the national average of $4.14 and about $1.10 higher than a year ago. AAA Mountain West spokesperson Aldo Vazquez attributed the spike to continued volatility near the Strait of Hormuz pushing crude oil into the $90-per-barrel range, offsetting the seasonal late-summer price dip. Despite the higher costs, AAA and Utah transportation officials expect heavy holiday travel, including to Arches and Zion national parks, and UDOT is forecasting delays of up to 60 minutes on some roads, worst on Monday as travelers return. UDOT plans to suspend construction and open lanes where possible, though some work zones in Spanish Fork and Provo canyons and near Thistle Junction will keep partial restrictions in place.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Church wins unanimous federal ruling in tithing case appeal
item.description: A three-judge panel of the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals unanimously affirmed a 2025 district court ruling dismissing a consolidated class-action lawsuit in which nine plaintiffs sought the return of tithing donations made to The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Judges Harris Hartz, Gregory Phillips and Nancy Moritz wrote that they saw no reversible error in U.S. District Judge Robert Shelby's April 2025 ruling that the plaintiffs, including Daniel Chappell, John Oaks and Masen Christensen, filed their claims after the three-year statute of limitations had expired. The plaintiffs, who had filed similar suits in Utah, California, Tennessee and Washington that were later consolidated, alleged the church fraudulently induced and misused donations; Shelby's dismissal was with prejudice, barring them from refiling. Church spokesman Sam Penrod said after Shelby's original ruling that tithing donations are carefully managed under church leaders' direction and that the claims were rightly dismissed.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch, Deseret News

item.title: Numerous bank cards, fake IDs found following fiery crash
item.description: St. George police booked Mitchell Steven Inclan, 33, on dozens of charges Thursday, following the earlier arrest of Stephen Michael Laughlin, 42, after the pair allegedly used a stolen BMW to flee police following a credit-card fraud spree at Red Cliffs Mall that ended when their car crashed and caught fire near an I-15 on-ramp. According to a police booking affidavit, the men were identified using mall surveillance footage and license plate readers after a victim reported his and his wife's stolen credit cards were used at multiple stores; when officers tried to stop the BMW, Laughlin sped away, and the two later swapped seats before crashing. Investigators recovered numerous fake ID cards bearing the men's photos under different identities, along with stolen mail, checks, 20 stolen bank cards, a printer, laptops and a stolen gun from the burned vehicle. Both men, believed to be from the Las Vegas area, face charges including theft, forgery, unlawful possession of bank cards and identification, and reckless driving.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: UVU students use AI to develop toothpaste business
item.description: Brothers Ben and Will Wright, students in Utah Valley University's first applied AI master's cohort, used artificial intelligence to research and formulate a new toothpaste line through their company Klyyr, motivated by their own history of cavities and root canals despite a healthy family background. The brothers said AI helped them quickly compare formulas and narrow in on ingredients, while food scientists and chemists made the final calls to ensure the product met safety standards. Ben Wright said toothpaste is just a starting point for a broader line of products they hope to develop. Will Wright emphasized that AI accelerates research but can't replace human expertise, since specialists must have the final say on formulation decisions.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: Man accused of pointed realistic looking gun at police 'for no apparent reason'
item.description: Gloire Seba, 30, was charged Thursday in 4th District Court with four counts of assault on an officer and other charges after police said he pointed a realistic-looking BB gun at officers near 100 South and 300 East while they were conducting an unrelated investigation. According to a police booking affidavit, Seba, who was wearing a bullet-resistant-style vest, had been interrupting the investigation with questions before getting into a nearby vehicle and raising a silver handgun toward officers while laughing; officers determined the weapon was a modified BB gun designed to closely resemble a real firearm. When questioned, Seba said he was "just showing" officers the barrel to prove it wasn't loaded, but prosecutors said the display created a potentially deadly confrontation. Prosecutors noted Seba has 37 prior arrests and 15 convictions, including two felonies, and said his actions represented an escalation of his criminal history.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: From struggle to recognition: How one mom's art made its way to Ogden's streets
item.description: Tawni Jae Sherlock, an Army veteran and Weber State University student, found healing from PTSD and personal trauma through Weber State's free Venture Course in the Humanities. Sherlock, who was born in Guam and moved to Utah in 2000 when her family relocated to Hill Air Force Base, says the class reconnected her to art after years of struggle. Inspired by an assignment to create surreal art tied to the Great Salt Lake, she made a piece called "Betsy" — a winged buffalo with a woman's face and cactus flowers — which was later selected for display on Ogden's public transit buses. Sherlock says the recognition has been a proud moment for her family, and she credits her instructors with encouraging her to pursue her education and future goals.
item.dc:creator: Tamara Vaifanua, KSL

item.title: 2 accused of taking shoes at gunpoint, firing shots
item.description: Two men with alleged gang ties, Aliga M. Malual, 22, of West Valley City, and Sandy Kuj, 18, of Salt Lake City, have been charged in 3rd District Court after an Aug. 21 robbery and shooting in a parking lot near 5500 West and 3500 South in West Valley City. Malual faces two counts of aggravated robbery, obstruction of justice, causing a riot, and three counts of discharge of a firearm, while Kuj faces the robbery, obstruction and riot charges. Police say they found three victims, two bullets and three shell casings at the scene; one victim said he was robbed of his belongings, including his shoes, and shot at, while another said several men confronted him before one pulled a gun. Malual reportedly told police his brother was being confronted by a group and he retrieved his gun before shots were fired, according to charging documents.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: People seek mental health benefits after Charlie Kirk shooting, officials say
item.description: Nearly a year after the fatal shooting of Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University, Utah state officials say dozens of people affected by the tragedy are still seeking mental health support through the state's victim compensation program. Office for Victims of Crime Director Chyleen Richey said 173 people have applied for compensation-funded mental health therapy, with eligibility extending beyond direct witnesses to anyone determined to have been in the "zone of danger," who qualify as primary victims for 25 therapy sessions. Mental health professionals, including Tangible Therapy CEO Brady Clegg, say trauma symptoms like nightmares and sleep difficulty can surface months after a traumatic event even for people who initially felt they had processed it. UVU President Jon Anderson said the university continues offering mental health resources to students affected by the shooting or by other personal struggles.
item.dc:creator: Annette Campbell, KSL

item.title: Bridgerland Technical College, USU partnership creates direct path from technical training to bachelor's degree
item.description: Bridgerland Technical College and Utah State University have launched a new partnership called "BTECH Now, USU Next," designed to give students a more direct path from hands-on technical training to a USU bachelor's degree. The program offers direct admission to Utah State, academic advising, established credit-transfer pathways and scholarship consideration, while letting students continue BTECH's career-focused training and even join Aggie student life before formally enrolling. BTECH interim president Lisa Moon and USU President Brad Mortensen said the agreement removes barriers and redundant applications between the schools, building on their long-standing relationship. Graduates Addison Egbert and Trevin Murray, who each separately completed both programs, said the streamlined pathway would have saved them time, money and the hassle of applying to both schools individually. The partnership took effect immediately after being signed.
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz, KSL

item.title: The sweet way a Utah donut shop is saving lives
item.description: The Other Side Village, a Salt Lake City nonprofit led by CEO Preston Cochrane, provides tiny homes and life-skills training to people transitioning out of homelessness, funding its work through social enterprises rather than fees or federal grants. One of those businesses, The Other Side Donuts near the tiny-home village on Redwood Road, employs program participants — including general manager Nicholas Smith, who has his own history of homelessness — as part of job training Cochrane calls an incubator for workplace skills. Applicants who have been homeless for at least 12 months (the average is nine years) can apply for the program, typically spending about nine months in a prep phase that includes working at the donut shop or another enterprise before qualifying for a fully furnished tiny home in the gated, 40-acre Poplar Grove community. The self-governed, sober community's first phase includes 60 homes plus shared services like a medical clinic, dental office and clubhouse, with residents expected to hold each other to a higher standard than they experienced while homeless.
item.dc:creator: Kathleen Clove, KSL

item.title: Tooele real estate agent charged with murdering girlfriend; friends say she was an 'amazing mom'
item.description: A Tooele real estate agent, identified in reports as Daniel Ruesga, has been charged with murder in the shooting death of his on-again, off-again girlfriend, Silvia Bahena, whose four children were home during the shooting and later found her body. Friends described Bahena, a nail artist who recently became a mortgage loan officer, as hardworking, talented and devoted to her children, while several said the relationship had a documented history of problems despite claims that Ruesga had changed. Court records show Ruesga pleaded no contest to a domestic-violence-enhanceable misdemeanor property damage charge in June 2025 and was ordered to complete a domestic-violence-related anger management course; a friend of Bahena's believes she was the victim in that earlier incident. Friends are now raising money to support Bahena's four children.
item.dc:creator: Garna Mejia, KSL

item.title: How Midway is preserving its small-town roots with annual Swiss Days
item.description: Midway's annual Swiss Days festival, now in its 79th year, has grown from a small local farmer's market into one of Utah's most-attended craft markets, drawing more than 300 vendor applications for roughly 160 juried, handmade-goods booths. Swiss Days committee member Aja Phillips, whose family has volunteered at the event for generations, said the entirely volunteer-run weekend — which includes a parade, 10K race, barbecue dinner and breakfast — helps preserve Midway's Swiss heritage through food like the iconic lemon yodel, Swiss and German music, and the youth Swiss Miss royalty program. As crowds have grown, organizers added a free shuttle service to ease parking congestion on the town's small streets. Phillips said despite the chaos, residents embrace the event as a chance to connect with neighbors and welcome visitors, reflecting Midway's small-town character even as the city continues to grow.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: National Park Services proposes a 'simpler' approach for bicycles, e-bikes at parks
item.description: The National Park Service is proposing a new rule that would give park superintendents authority to designate additional locations — including administrative roads and trails — for bicycle and e-bike use across all national parks, including Utah's "Mighty 5." The rule would keep the existing ban on using an e-bike's motor alone for extended propulsion except where motor vehicles are already permitted, and would still let superintendents impose safety- or resource-based restrictions. NPS comptroller Jessica Bowron said the proposal creates a "simpler, more consistent approach" to bike access system-wide, aligning with efficiency and accessibility executive orders signed by President Trump; the agency also cited benefits like reduced vehicle congestion and expanded access for people limited by age, illness, disability or terrain. The rule is open for public comment through Nov. 2, and some commenters, including mountain bikers, have urged a science-based, trail-by-trail approach rather than blanket access.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Midvale neighbors said man chose dead-end street as he fled from police
item.description: A man was arrested in Midvale Wednesday after a brief police pursuit ended when he crashed his car into a tree on a dead-end street near 420 East and 7200 South, according to Unified Police Sgt. Aymee Race. Race said officers tried to stop an erratically driven vehicle near 7100 S. State St. around 12:50 p.m., but the driver crashed into an officer before fleeing through neighborhood backyards. Neighbors said the suspect ran into a nearby family's home, swapped his shirt for one of the children's, grabbed a scooter, and fled toward a nearby canal, where an officer jumped a fence and caught him. Police arrested 39-year-old Jeffrey Levie on suspicion of fleeing from police, aggravated assault on a police officer and burglary.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: 'We will tell their stories': Friends, family gather to remember father, daughter killed in crash
item.description: About 150 friends, family and community members gathered in Ogden on Wednesday evening for a vigil honoring Jody Thackeray and his daughter Desiree Thackeray, who died a week earlier in a crash on I-215. Speakers, including Jody's daughter Rebecca Vigil Perez and his coworker Christina Reynosa from Fresenius Medical Care, remembered Jody as someone who made everyone laugh and celebrated coworkers' birthdays with a signature dance, while friends like Reyna Grijalva described 40-year-old Desiree as a warm, loving presence who treated friends like family. One attendee said Jody, his stepfather, had been more of a father figure to him than his own biological father. Organizers also raised money to help cover household bills and expenses left behind, while friend Lacey Trujillo led attendees in a pledge to keep telling Jody and Desiree's stories and honor their memory.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Semitruck driver hospitalized after rolling, falling down embankment in Daggett County
item.description: A semitruck driver hauling water was hospitalized Wednesday morning after crashing on state Route 44 near Manila in Daggett County, the Utah Highway Patrol said. UHP said the truck went off the road to the left around 10:30 a.m., rolled, slid through a guardrail and fell down a steep embankment, traveling roughly 300 feet in the process. The driver, the semitruck's only occupant, was flown to the hospital by medical helicopter, and a section of Route 44 was briefly closed before reopening. Authorities have not released the driver's condition or said what caused the crash.
item.dc:creator: Devin Oldroyd, KSL

item.title: Democrat exits Utah state Senate race, backs Forward Party candidate
item.description: Democrat Mackenzie Miller, a Navy veteran, dropped out of Utah's Senate District 11 race last week and is now backing Forward Party incumbent Sen. Emily Buss over Republican challenger Brooks Benson in the November election. Miller said in a social media post that he made the decision after finding organizations reluctant to fund a three-way race, choosing instead to give Buss the resources to keep a Republican from winning the seat, while pledging to keep fighting for "a better Utah." Forward Party Chairman Phil Boileau said the new head-to-head race gives voters a chance to reject "partisan politics-as-usual," and Buss said she answers "only to the voters, not party insiders." Benson said his priorities include cutting government waste, lowering taxes, opposing government mass surveillance and improving road infrastructure in the district, with Election Day set for Nov. 3.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Utah company aims to turn homeownership into an employee benefit
item.description: Provo entrepreneur Cheri Salazar founded NestSteps, a startup that turns homeownership assistance into an employee benefit by offering a financial management platform, 401(k)-style employer contribution plans toward down payments, and homebuying education and coaching. The company makes money through platform fees and referral fees from real estate agents, and Salazar said NestSteps is currently working with 11 Utah companies, with strong employee interest — one recent employer meeting led to 58 people signing up immediately afterward. Jared Bowen, 24, an early participant in the program, is closing on his first home in Saratoga Springs this week and credited NestSteps' education with giving him confidence that buying a home was achievable. Salazar said she believes the benefit fills a gap that's long been missing from employer benefits packages.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: 'It's more than just a house': Multi-generational Springdale family picking up pieces after flood
item.description: A multi-generational family in Springdale is recovering after flash flooding from Zion National Park sent several feet of water into the basement of their uninsured "dome house" Monday afternoon. Homeowner Sheralyn Madsen, who moved into the geodesic-dome home with her parents in 1986 and has lived there for 40 years across six generations of family history, said the flood destroyed decades of sentimental belongings and called the loss "more than just a house" — a sanctuary where her children and grandchildren were born. Madsen's daughter Glazier wasn't home when the water rose but got a call describing water coming into a bedroom, and later had trouble reaching her husband amid limited cell service during the storm. With no insurance to cover the damage, the family — including Madsen's father, who is recovering from recent open-heart surgery — is now relying on each other and community support while assessing the losses and hoping to rebuild.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: EPA proposals to speed up data center projects 'anti-democratic,' according to Utah environmental group
item.description: The EPA has proposed removing the federal requirement for public comment in air-quality permitting for projects like data centers, instead leaving that decision to individual states, raising concern among Utah environmental groups even though Utah Division of Air Quality director Bryce Bird said the state has no plans to change its own public-input process. Dr. Brian Moench of Utah Physicians for a Healthy Environment worries the rule change would leave the door open for a future governor to eliminate public input by directive, even if Utah doesn't act on it now. Bird noted that regardless of the public-comment change, EPA air-quality standards and pollution-control technology requirements would remain in place. A second EPA proposal would let construction on data center and power plant projects begin before air-quality permits are issued, which Moench called "anti-democratic," saying it would be nearly impossible to stop a project already built by the time the public could weigh in. Public comment periods for both proposals closed last month, and the EPA is reviewing feedback before a final decision.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: Lawsuits filed over reduction of 2 Utah national monuments, rekindling legal battle
item.description: Several conservation groups, including the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance and Sierra Club, filed lawsuits Wednesday in U.S. District Court seeking to void both President Trump's July order shrinking Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante national monuments to about 121,000 and 182,000 acres, and his original 2017 reduction order. The groups argue the Antiquities Act lets presidents create monuments but not eliminate protections or override boundaries Congress has confirmed, with Sierra Club's Athan Manuel saying Trump "cannot erase America's national monuments with the stroke of a pen." Utah Republican leaders, including Gov. Spencer Cox, have praised the reductions as "rightsizing" the monuments, and Interior deputy secretary Kate MacGregor pointed to smaller historical monument designations in defending the move, though conservation groups noted other historical monuments were far larger. SUWA legal director Steve Bloch said the groups will also watch for "on-the-ground mischief" like new mining claims — nine of which were reportedly filed within a month of the order — and illegal vehicle use in areas that lost protected status, with no set timeline for how the new lawsuits will play out.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Have You Seen This? Waterfalls caused by flooding in Zion National Park
item.description: Intense storms that hit parts of Utah Monday triggered flash floods in Zion National Park that created striking waterfalls cascading off the park's Navajo Sandstone cliffs, as captured in viewer videos shared by KSL meteorologist Matt Johnson. Footage showed the flooding along state Route 9, where the runoff was both visually dramatic and damaging, unsettling visitors in the park at the time. Johnson noted that while the floods caused real damage, water and erosion are also what originally carved Zion's canyons, framing the waterfalls as nature continuing that same erosive process.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: Man accused of stalking, impersonating officer
item.description: A 55-year-old Salt Lake City man, Jack C. Rockefeller, was charged Tuesday in 4th District Court with stalking and impersonating an officer after allegedly harassing an Orem man he met on a dating app. According to charging documents, the two began an intimate relationship after meeting online, but Rockefeller later told the man he had a warrant out for his arrest and would be used as a scapegoat in an investigation. On Aug. 12, Rockefeller reportedly showed up at the man's workplace and later his home claiming to be a U.S. Marshal with an arrest warrant, sent photos to the man's family calling him a "horrible person" who needed an attorney, and called the man's property manager falsely claiming to be a federal agent investigating him for methamphetamine distribution. Orem police confirmed Rockefeller was not a real officer and that no warrant existed for the victim.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Delta Sigma Theta volunteers transform Franklin Elementary School with a day at play
item.description: More than 300 Delta Sigma Theta sorority volunteers gathered at Franklin Elementary School in Salt Lake City on Wednesday to renovate the playground and paint a community mural as part of the sorority's Impact Day of Service. Regional director Kimberly M. Usher said the sorority makes community investment a standard part of kicking off its conferences, and Utah state Rep. Sandra Hollins, D-Salt Lake City, said Franklin Elementary was chosen because it serves a lower- to moderate-income community, reflecting Delta's philosophy of not just holding a conference and leaving. International director Cheryl W. Turner said the group wanted an elementary school that could show kids the importance of exercise and having an active gathering place. The service project kicked off the sorority's Farwest Regional Conference, which is bringing more than 1,500 attendees to Salt Lake City through Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: Intermountain Health to relocate LDS Hospital in Salt Lake City
item.description: Intermountain Health's board has approved relocating LDS Hospital from its longtime home in Salt Lake City's Avenues neighborhood to a new site near 754 South State Street, land the health system purchased nearly five years ago. Officials said Wednesday they hope to break ground by the end of the year, with construction expected to take three to five years once underway. Plans filed with the city describe a multi-building campus, with the tallest structure topping out at just over 200 feet. Intermountain has not yet decided what will happen to the century-old Avenues hospital, though it may retain some services there, and Salt Lake County Mayor Jenny Wilson and several County Council members have pushed for the new facility to expand behavioral health inpatient capacity beyond what LDS Hospital currently offers.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: St. George man hospitalized with rare, severe form of West Nile virus, wife says
item.description: Washington County resident Tammy Gill is warning others about West Nile virus after her husband, Kevin Gill, developed a rare neuroinvasive form of the disease that she says nearly killed him. She believes he was bitten by a mosquito while the couple grilled on their patio, and within days he had a 102-degree fever, neck pain and facial redness that worsened until he suffered a seizure and, doctors later found, a stroke. Utah County Health Department nursing director Michael Leman said neuroinvasive West Nile affects the central nervous system in only about 1% of cases but can be fatal roughly 10% of the time, with symptoms including muscle weakness, disorientation and seizures. Leman noted a separate Utah County case initially flagged as neuroinvasive was later determined not to meet that threshold after further review.
item.dc:creator: Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: 1M reserved tickets for Salt Lake Temple open house
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints announced that the first million reservations for the Salt Lake Temple open house were claimed within 24 hours of becoming available. Reservations opened Tuesday on TempleSquare.org and the Temple Square app after church leaders unveiled the celebration's theme, “Rejoice in Christ,” at a media event, with President Dieter F. Uchtdorf of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles speaking about the church's global reach. More reservations are expected to be released, though the church has not said when. The Salt Lake Temple Celebration, including open house tours and additional exhibits around Temple Square, will run from April 5 through Oct. 1, 2027.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Salt Lake City man charged with killing girlfriend in Tooele
item.description: Daniel Castro Ruesga, 37, of Salt Lake City has been charged with murder and related counts after Tooele police say he intentionally crashed his pickup into his girlfriend's Tesla and then shot her inside the vehicle in a garage. Officers responding to a shots-fired call just before midnight Monday found the vehicles collided and the victim, since identified on social media as 37-year-old Silvia Bahena, dead in the driver's seat. According to a police booking affidavit, Ruesga admitted after being read his Miranda rights to crashing into the car and shooting Bahena following an argument, and the affidavit states her four children were inside the home and heard the incident before finding their mother. Ruesga faces one count of murder, four counts of domestic violence in the presence of a child, and a misdemeanor firearm discharge charge.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Stabbing on TRAX train causes delays in Salt Lake City
item.description: A person was stabbed twice aboard a northbound Blue Line TRAX train near 600 South Main Street in Salt Lake City on Wednesday morning, according to the Utah Transit Authority and Salt Lake City police. UTA said two strangers got into a fight in which one allegedly stabbed the other, who was taken to the hospital in stable condition. The incident forced delays across the Red, Green and Blue TRAX lines, and UTA put a bridge bus in place between the Gallivan Plaza and the Ballpark and Library stations while officers investigated.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Armed man shot by Salt Lake City police identified
item.description: Salt Lake City police have arrested 37-year-old Dallas Clint Fowers on charges including assault on an officer, criminal mischief and failing to stop for police, days after he was shot by responding officers. According to a booking affidavit, officers were called to a Burger King on 400 South Monday night over a report of an intoxicated, incoherent man vandalizing a car, and body camera footage allegedly shows Fowers holding a knife and refusing repeated commands to drop it and get on the ground. Officers deployed Taser prongs that did not stop him, and he ran through nearby parking lots before being shot, the affidavit states.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: ICE arrest in Ogden as police officer looks on sparks intense City Council discussion
item.description: Ogden Mayor Ben Nadolski told the City Council Tuesday that a policy governing police interactions with federal immigration authorities is in the works, a week after a viral incident in which an Ogden officer stood by during an ICE agent's arrest of a man from Venezuela. The meeting drew numerous residents pressing for clearer guidelines or criticizing the federal immigration crackdown, including Kim Haslam, who called for defined rules on what Ogden police can and cannot do when an ICE operation intersects with a call for service. City Council member Kevin Lundell had recorded video of the original Aug. 25 encounter, and the Ogden Police Department later released the officer's body camera footage; resident Emily Fox told the council the perceived cooperation with ICE has damaged public trust in police. Nadolski did not give a timeline for the policy, and his comments were briefly interrupted by an audience member demanding one.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Utah father remembered for helping others before fatal lightning strike in Florida
item.description: Family and friends are mourning Steve Matheson, a Utah husband and father killed by a lightning strike while helping stranded boaters during a sudden storm off the Florida coast on Aug. 29. Matheson had extended a work trip to spend time with childhood best friend David Cole, and the two were returning from a day of jet skiing when they stopped to help a boat stuck on a sandbar as a severe thunderstorm intensified around them. Cole said Matheson was reluctant to risk the weather but wanted to get home safely to his wife and children, and moments after the pair assisted the stranded boaters, Matheson was struck by lightning. Cole described their decades-long friendship, dating back to age 4, and said he is heartbroken by the sudden loss.
item.dc:creator: Annette Campbell, KSL

item.title: Southern Utah University interns recognized for helping rescue hiker in Arizona
item.description: Three college interns — Brooklyn Bauer and Jake McDonald, working with the Bureau of Land Management's Kanab Field Office, and University of Wyoming student Conner Buchanan — received a “Life Saver Award” for helping a 67-year-old woman suffering heat exhaustion on The Wave trail near the Utah-Arizona border in July. The interns, part of Southern Utah University's Intergovernmental Internship Cooperative, provided cooling towels, electrolytes and shade before McDonald contacted the Coconino County Sheriff's Office to request a rescue helicopter. When an incoming storm made helicopter evacuation impossible, McDonald and arriving paramedics walked the woman back to the parking lot for further treatment. All three credited their internship's emergency-response training for preparing them to act quickly.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: A new way to reach Arches National Park is now available from Moab
item.description: A new Moab-to-Arches shuttle launched Tuesday, offering free rides between downtown Moab and the Arches National Park visitor center for anyone holding a valid national park pass. The bus runs on 15- to 30-minute intervals from four Moab pickup points between roughly 8 a.m. and 5 p.m., and once inside the park riders can transfer to shuttles serving popular trailheads like Delicate Arch and the Windows. The pilot, funded by $1.5 million each from state transportation officials and Grand County alongside a matching National Park Service award, will run through Oct. 31 and again from March through June 2027 before local leaders decide on a permanent service. Grand County leaders pushed for the shuttle after criticizing the park's timed-entry system, which a University of Utah Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute study found had reduced Arches visitation by roughly 14%.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Child hit by baseball in Henefer, hospitalized; coach helps save life
item.description: A youth baseball coach's quick CPR likely saved the life of a child who suffered a medical emergency after being struck by a baseball during practice at Henefer Town Park Tuesday evening, according to the North Summit Fire District. The coach began chest compressions before first responders arrived, and paramedics continued lifesaving efforts on scene, including using a defibrillator to restore the child's pulse. The child was flown by medical helicopter to Intermountain Primary Children's Hospital for further treatment. The fire district said the incident underscores the importance of bystander CPR and AED training, and the child's identity has not been released.
item.dc:creator: Devin Oldroyd, KSL

item.title: 'It's been hard': Sandy man speaks out on behalf of cousin facing death in Iran for protesting
item.description: Masoud Nourmohammadi, a naturalized U.S. citizen living in Sandy, is speaking publicly to draw attention to his twin cousins, Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, who were jailed in Iran after taking part in anti-government protests in January. Nourmohammadi said Taraneh, now 20, was sentenced to death this week while Romina received a 25-year prison term, and he plans to seek support from Utah's congressional delegation. Human rights groups including Hengaw, based in Norway, and outlets such as Radio Free Europe have reported on the case, with Hengaw saying the sisters and others were convicted on charges including “waging war against God” and “propaganda against the state.” Nourmohammadi said the sisters now have access to human rights lawyers attempting to appeal the death sentence, though he is uncertain what to expect from Iran's judicial process.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: After crash, Utah driver finds big difference in repair estimates
item.description: Salt Lake City driver Collin Holbrook says insurer USAA initially paid only a $1,444.66 repair estimate from its “preferred” body shop after he was rear-ended over Memorial Day weekend, then balked at a second shop's more thorough $5,491.34 estimate, arguing the extra damage came from a different crash. After the KSL Investigators contacted USAA on his behalf and laid out a detailed timeline, the insurer asked to inspect Holbrook's car and review his evidence, and about a week later paid the roughly $4,000 difference. USAA confirmed the additional damage was ultimately validated. Utah Insurance Department Commissioner Jon Pike said drivers should photograph damage extensively and get multiple repair bids — he suggested at least three — and noted Utah law does not require using an insurer's preferred shop.
item.dc:creator: Matt Gephardt, KSL

item.title: Lightning strike damages Hyrum front yard, knocks out power and natural gas line
item.description: A lightning strike to a tree in Hyrum Monday night sent electrical current into the ground, melting an underground natural gas line and forcing a neighborhood evacuation, according to homeowner Jean Cefalo and Hyrum City Light & Power's Blake Ballard. Cefalo said the strike felt like it lifted her house off the ground, and residents had to leave on foot rather than by vehicle once they smelled gas. The strike also knocked out power to nearby homes, and utility crews spent much of Tuesday repairing the gas and electrical lines. No one was injured and no structures caught fire, and power was restored by Tuesday.
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz, KSL

item.title: Utah becomes first state to roll out digital platform for authenticating documents
item.description: Utah's Office of the Lieutenant Governor is rolling out the nation's first statewide digital apostille program this week, allowing residents to authenticate documents like diplomas, birth certificates and corporate paperwork online instead of mailing them or visiting the Capitol in person. Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson said demand for apostilles has grown sharply, from about 18,000 documents authenticated in 2020 to more than 45,000 in the past fiscal year, and the digital certificates carry the same legal weight in more than 100 countries under a 1961 international treaty. Digital authentication is not yet available for vital records such as birth certificates because those documents are printed on security paper that displays “void” when copied, according to Chris Jackson, CEO of @Gov, the company behind the program, who said his firm is working with state agencies to eventually close that gap.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Utah woman gets help from 'The Doctor' to announce her cancer remission
item.description: South Jordan resident Katie Walterman, a longtime “Doctor Who” fan, was diagnosed with Stage 4 uterine cancer in 2024 after months of symptoms including bloating and menstrual changes led to a hysterectomy that revealed extensive cancerous growths. She underwent aggressive chemotherapy and radiation at the Huntsman Cancer Institute's Daybreak location, crediting her husband, family and medical team for helping her through treatment. Though doctors typically avoid calling Stage 4 cancer patients cancer-free, Walterman's care team found a meaningful way to help her mark reaching that milestone tied to her favorite show. She described the moment as feeling like providence after a grueling fight.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Grand Canyon flooding deals another blow to family-owned landmark
item.description: Deadly flash flooding in the Grand Canyon that killed two people and left one hiker still missing has also hit the finances of the century-old Jacob Lake Inn on the North Rim. Owner Melinda Rich Marshall said the business has lost roughly 70 reservations since Sunday night heading into what is normally one of its busiest weekends of the year, with occupancy now below 50%. Grand Canyon Historical Society vice president Davy Crockett called the flooding historic, noting the last comparable event was in 1966, and suggested debris from a prior wildfire may have worsened this year's flood. Marshall said her family is seeking federal assistance while emphasizing that the North Rim and the inn remain open to visitors.
item.dc:creator: Dan Rascon, KSL

item.title: WATCH LIVE: Theme unveiled for Salt Lake Temple Celebration, reservations become available
item.description: KSL previewed Tuesday's Salt Lake Temple Celebration event, at which reservations for the 2027 open house became available and church leaders revealed the celebration's theme during a livestreamed event featuring a children's choir. Reservations opened through TempleSquare.org and the Temple Square app at 11 a.m., released in phases so unavailable time slots would have other openings later. Free tours of the newly restored Salt Lake Temple are set to run from 8:40 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily except Sunday, when they begin at noon, with the celebration spanning April 5 through Oct. 1, 2027. Individuals can reserve up to six tickets each, and officials expect millions of visitors during the celebration, the first public tours of the historic temple since 1893.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: 'He is going to kill somebody': Serial arsonist sentenced for June fire in Tooele County
item.description: Timothy West, 39, a former volunteer firefighter with a history of arson, was sentenced Monday to three consecutive zero-to-five-year prison terms after pleading guilty to setting a June fire near Stockton that forced evacuations. Tooele County prosecutor Gary Searle told the judge West has now been convicted of arson in four separate cases, including a 2014 wildfire that burned about 200 acres and contaminated Stockton's water supply. Audio from a 2015 parole hearing showed West had been diagnosed with pyromania, and he told a hearing officer at the time he planned to control the impulse by lighting candles instead. Third District Judge Douglas Hogan said the sentence gives the Board of Pardons and Parole authority to hold West for up to 15 years, acknowledging he did not have an answer for how to fix West's behavior.
item.dc:creator: Daniella Rivera, KSL

item.title: Tooele woman found dead in vehicle; boyfriend arrested
item.description: A 37-year-old Tooele man, Daniel Ruesga, was arrested overnight and booked on suspicion of murder and domestic violence charges after his girlfriend was found fatally shot in her vehicle. Police responding to a shots-fired call near 600 E. Kings Landing Road found a pickup truck, registered to Ruesga, crashed into the back of a Tesla in a garage, with the woman dead in the driver's seat. According to a booking affidavit, Ruesga admitted after a Miranda warning that he intentionally crashed into the vehicle and shot the woman multiple times following an argument. The victim's four children were inside the home and heard the shooting before finding their mother dead; her name had not been released as of Tuesday morning.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Clinton man sentenced to prison in 2021 shooting of woman in Roy
item.description: A 4th District judge sentenced Brayden Daniel Coles, 36, to one-to-15 years in prison on three second-degree felony counts for a 2021 shooting outside a Roy convenience store that wounded a woman near her ribcage. Judge Cristina Ortega ordered the sentences served concurrently and closed four related misdemeanor counts with credit for 381 days already served. A jury convicted Coles in March after a four-day trial following a September 2021 confrontation in which he fired five shots at the woman, and he was later tracked down in Clinton via an ankle monitor. His attorney has filed notice of an appeal of both the conviction and the sentence.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Beaver hoping to avoid new problems after catastrophic flooding in July
item.description: Beaver Mayor Matt Robinson said Monday that many families remain displaced by catastrophic July 19 flooding that heavily damaged the city's "Grove" neighborhood, even as a new round of thunderstorms threatened the area without causing new flooding. Robinson, whose parents and a brother still live in the Grove, said a couple of homes could ultimately be declared total losses while repairs continue elsewhere. City and county crews have spent weeks clearing river-channel debris and shoring up banks, which Robinson said seems to be helping water and mud move more freely than on the day of the original flood. He cautioned that the risk of another flooding event remains high in the coming months and years regardless of this week's forecast.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: No tornado, but central Utah wind event generated 100 mph wind gusts, NWS says
item.description: The National Weather Service determined that a storm which tore through Millard County near Lynndyl on Saturday was not a tornado, but straight-line winds that peaked between 80 and 100 mph over a path more than 17 miles long. The wind and hail toppled nearly three dozen empty rail cars, stripped trees, shredded a nearby cornfield nearing harvest, and caused extensive siding, window and roof damage to homes, according to the agency's report. Meteorologist Alex DeSmet said the assessment relied on damage surveys, radar review, resident interviews and photos, with some damage consistent with EF-1-level 100 mph winds despite insufficient evidence of a tornado touchdown. Utah Rep. Celeste Maloy, Attorney General Derek Brown and Utah Farm Bureau vice president Wade Garrett toured the damage Sunday to gauge how the community near Lynndyl could get assistance.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Flash flooding strands family in Capitol Reef
item.description: A family camping at Capitol Reef National Park's Fruita campground got stranded overnight in Cathedral Valley after a nearby creek bed rose roughly three feet in about 15 minutes during Saturday's storms, according to camper Barry Cann. Cann said the group waited out the flood rather than risk driving across the rising water and sticky clay mud, and one member used a phone's satellite texting feature to reach emergency services, who advised them to wait it out since they had enough food and water. The family camped in their vehicles overnight and made it out safely the next morning once the water receded, using their car to power through the muddy riverbank. Cann, who grew up exploring Utah's deserts but had never experienced a flash flood before, described the ordeal as disconcerting given the uncertainty about how the weather would continue to develop.
item.dc:creator: Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: Tyler Robinson may learn today if he will stand trial for allegedly killing Charlie Kirk
item.description: Tyler Robinson, 23, charged with aggravated murder and six other counts in the fatal shooting of conservative activist Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University last September, was scheduled for closing arguments Tuesday in a preliminary hearing before 4th District Judge Tony Graf, who was expected to rule on whether the case proceeds to trial. Prosecutors have said they will seek the death penalty if Robinson is bound over and convicted, and in July presented surveillance video, messages attributed to Robinson and testimony from his roommate as evidence tying him to the shooting. Robinson's defense challenged the reliability of DNA testing and argued much of the state's evidence is inadmissible hearsay, while also fighting to keep cameras out of the courtroom and part of a recent filing sealed, citing concerns about tainting a future jury pool. The defense separately reported it is still working through an enormous volume of digital evidence, including a hard drive with roughly 12.1 terabytes of forensic data extracted from six mobile devices and 14 computer images.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Semi-tractor driver charged in Saratoga Springs crash that killed 13-year-old boy
item.description: Michael Lynn Fowers, 53, of Genola, was charged Monday with manslaughter and four counts of reckless endangerment after prosecutors said his semi-tractor towing two dump trailers ran a red light in Saratoga Springs in May and struck a minivan, killing 13-year-old Parker Samuel Gale. Charging documents say Fowers, traveling 40 mph in a 50 mph zone, entered the Pony Express Parkway and Mountainview Corridor intersection eight seconds after the light turned red and did not brake before the collision. Parker was in the front passenger seat with three younger siblings in back; he died in the hospital days later, while his mother suffered serious injuries and a 10-year-old sibling suffered a concussion. Fowers initially told police he thought the light was green, but dash-cam video and witnesses contradicted that account, according to the charges.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Residents recount 'destruction' of Springdale flooding
item.description: Flash flooding tore through Springdale on Monday, sending mud and debris across roads and flooding homes near Zion National Park, including the basement level of Angelea and Jacob Glazier's multi-generation family home, where floodwaters broke a window and left a four-foot water line in a boys' bedroom. Glazier said she rushed home with her children as the water rose, watching belongings -- including her wedding dress -- wash away, and that about 30 volunteers later showed up to help salvage what they could. Visitors Marisol and Casey Woodward said they left the Narrows early after seeing storm warnings, only to encounter rockfall, a waterfall bursting over a cliffside and mud transforming roadside areas into small lakes as they drove out. A GoFundMe has been set up to help the Glazier family recover, and Glazier said she remained worried about further flooding as more storms moved through Monday evening.
item.dc:creator: Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: Man shot by police, in serious condition in Salt Lake
item.description: Salt Lake City police shot and seriously wounded a man near 600 East and 400 South Monday night after he displayed what officers called psychotic behavior, running into traffic and striking cars and windshields. Police said officers found the man armed with a knife when they arrived and that he refused to put it down before they opened fire. The man is expected to survive his injuries, and police said the incident remained under investigation as of Monday night. Authorities did not release his name or additional details about what preceded the encounter.
item.dc:creator: Devin Oldroyd, KSL

item.title: Flooding impacts Utah one last time to close out meteorological summer
item.description: Utah closed out its meteorological summer Monday with a wet finish, as multiple flash flood warnings, flood advisories and severe thunderstorm warnings stretched from Heber City and Nephi to St. George and Lake Powell through the day. A gauge on the North Fork of the Virgin River at Springdale spiked to 5,920 cubic feet per second, its fifth-highest reading on record, while a nearby water-height sensor jumped from 7 to 14 feet within an hour amid flooding that reached homes in the community. KSL meteorologist Matt Johnson said the storms formed when tropical moisture merged with a low-pressure system over Arizona, and Salt Lake City ended the season with 2.57 inches of rain, above its 2-inch norm, with more than 90% of that falling after July 20. Despite the wet finish, officials said more than 90% of Utah remained in at least severe drought, and additional tropical moisture is expected to reach the state by Labor Day weekend.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: 2 people dead, 1 missing from Grand Canyon flooding
item.description: Grand Canyon National Park officials confirmed a second death Monday from weekend flash flooding and debris flows in the Bright Angel Creek area that had trapped more than 80 hikers, with one person still missing as of Monday evening. Incident commander Dave Black said 82 people were rescued by hiking out or helicopter, and the missing-persons count had narrowed from roughly 30 unaccounted-for permit holders to just one after further searching. Officials said the flooding, tied to the same moisture pattern that hit Utah over the weekend, appears to have triggered a debris flow over last year's Dragon Bravo Fire burn scar, damaging about 40% of the Transcanyon Waterline. The park has closed Phantom Ranch, Bright Angel Campground and the North Kaibab Trail to Phantom Ranch, shut down overnight hotel accommodations including El Tovar and Bright Angel Lodge, and imposed Stage 4 water restrictions limiting showers and requiring conservation across the South Rim.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Meteorite from 'once-in-a-lifetime' Great Salt Lake crash on display at University of Utah
item.description: A 774-gram fragment of the Great Salt Lake meteorite, recovered after an August 2022 fireball event that boomed across the Salt Lake Valley, is now on permanent public display at the University of Utah's Sutton Building. U. geology research professor James Karner, who heard the fireball from his own driveway despite years of hunting meteorites in Antarctica, said advances in Doppler radar tracking over the past two decades let scientists and a NASA Johnson Space Center colleague pinpoint where fragments likely fell using weather data from Salt Lake City and Pocatello. The fragment, found by Arizona meteorite hunter Robert Ward, is the largest of roughly 3.2 kilograms recovered from the event and is only Utah's second witnessed, or "fall," meteorite after one near Garland in 1950. Karner said tracking the fireball's pre-impact trajectory let scientists match it to a specific asteroid family, something accomplished for only about 70 meteorites worldwide, and called the 4.56-billion-year-old rock one of the oldest objects most people will ever encounter.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Fake name, real bill: Former Taylorsville mayor charged twice under two different names
item.description: Former Taylorsville mayor Janice Rasmussen spent months fighting duplicate hospital bills after Intermountain Medical Center assigned her the alias "Brickred Cimmorden" when she arrived unable to give her name following a January hit-and-run outside a Sandy diner. Rasmussen paid her bills under her real name, but months later began receiving matching bills under the alias from Utah Emergency Physicians, the ER doctors' group, even after she mailed and faxed proof of payment. Group administrator Dr. David Barnes told KSL's Matt Gephardt the alias chart was never properly merged with Rasmussen's real record before discharge, and the billing company didn't recognize it as a duplicate, calling the mix-up a rare failure in a process that usually resolves before a trauma patient leaves the hospital. After KSL's inquiry, Utah Emergency Physicians apologized, canceled the phantom bill, and said it has since worked with its billing company to better flag alias accounts.
item.dc:creator: Matt Gephardt, KSL

item.title: Orangeville prepares for more rain after weekend flooding forces families from homes
item.description: Orangeville crews and residents spent Monday clearing debris from Cottonwood Creek and sandbagging homes ahead of possible additional rain, days after Saturday's flooding sent the creek surging roughly 15 feet and forced about 20 families to evacuate. Emery County Emergency Manager Jeremy Lake said longtime residents told him they'd never seen that much water in the creek, and city officials warned some evacuated families may not be able to return home for days due to water damage. Mayor Shaun Bell said he was worried further heavy rain could overwhelm the town's preparation efforts, while Emery County Commissioner Jordan Leonard noted the irony of a drought-stricken area suddenly getting all its rain at once. Lake said more than 100 volunteers turned out to fill sandbags, with people arriving from Huntington, Ferron and Castle Dale to help their neighbors.
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: Mexican man investigated for Ponzi scheme sentenced to deportation
item.description: Christian Montiel-Caleit, 45, a previously deported Mexican national living in West Valley City, was sentenced to time served and turned over to ICE last week after pleading guilty to illegal reentry in connection with a roughly $1 million Ponzi scheme run out of Utah. Federal prosecutors said Montiel-Caleit, unlicensed to sell securities, collected money from about 30 investors starting in 2021 by promising high returns funded by newer investors' contributions, with payouts drying up by December 2024. He generated apparent returns in part by flipping vehicles and real estate and issuing high-interest loans, according to the indictment, and had been removed from the U.S. once before in 2006 without authorization to reenter. Other charges, including securities fraud, wire fraud and money laundering, were dropped as part of his July plea agreement.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Spanish Fork residents frustrated after mayor voices approval of data center proposal
item.description: Spanish Fork Mayor Mike Mendenhall drew resident backlash after publicly voicing support for Volition, a Provo company proposing a self-powered AI data center at the former Fingerhut warehouse site, following a six-hour Aug. 18 public hearing where dozens of residents raised concerns about the project. Volition CEO Jeff Chavez said the facility would use natural-gas fuel cells operating in electrical isolation from the grid, with lower emissions, heat and water use than typical data centers, while the city considered a text amendment setting noise, water and air-quality rules and capping such sites at two citywide; the council ultimately tabled the issue. Mendenhall's social-media posts backing the plan drew hundreds of critical comments, with residents arguing the city should heed clear opposition rather than an "experimental industry," and some faulting the mayor's flippant replies to critics. The City Council was set to revisit the proposed data center rules and a development agreement with Volition on Tuesday.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Utah state park cancels beloved apple harvest following harsh season
item.description: Wasatch Mountain State Park canceled this year's beloved apple harvest at the historic Huber Grove orchard in Midway after a warm winter followed by hard April and May freezes wiped out most of the crop, park manager Jonathan Hunt said. USU Extension horticulturist Ben Scow said the same freeze created a statewide "fruit famine," with 95-100% losses reported for apricots, cherries, plums, peaches, pears and apples, prompting Gov. Spencer Cox to declare an agricultural emergency in 10 counties, though not Wasatch County. Only five or six of Huber Grove's roughly 80 trees, some dating to the 1800s, still bore any apples this year, far too few to support the event that normally draws at least 150 groups to pick a bushel apiece. Hunt said the park hopes for a better harvest next year and encouraged visitors to still enjoy the park's fall foliage and mountain biking trails in the meantime.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams and Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: Is the sky falling in college sports? Here's what Utahns think
item.description: A new Deseret News/Hinckley Institute of Politics poll found Utahns split on how they feel about college athletics' shift toward player pay and free movement between schools, with paying athletes through NIL and revenue sharing topping the list of concerns at 20%, followed by rising ticket costs, frequent transfers and conference realignment. Despite 56% expressing some worry, nearly a third of respondents said none of the changes bothered them, and attendance and viewership have kept climbing regardless. Age shaped opinions: baby boomers worried most about athlete pay, while Gen Z respondents were more bothered by transfer frequency. The poll also found Utahns nearly evenly split on whether revenue sharing will strengthen or weaken college sports long-term (39% vs. 29%), with younger voters more optimistic. Sports-business analyst David Carter and former Utah head coach Kyle Whittingham, now at Michigan, both weighed in on the sustainability of rising athlete pay.
item.dc:creator: Dennis Romboy, Deseret News

item.title: Sandy pulls $20K in Callaway gear after ad backlash
item.description: Sandy Mayor Monica Zoltanski ordered about $20,000 in Callaway merchandise pulled from the pro shop at the city's River Oaks Golf Course after a since-deleted Aug. 21 ad from Callaway and Good Good Golf drew backlash for showing co-founder Garrett Clark shoving golfer Alexis Miestowski. Clark apologized on Instagram, calling the ad -- meant as a parody of the movie "Obsession" -- a bad idea, while Callaway apologized separately and pledged $1 million toward organizations addressing violence against women. The fallout also cost Good Good its partnership with Callaway and a planned PGA Tour Austin sponsorship, and retailers including Dick's Sporting Goods and Target dropped Good Good products, though Callaway gear stayed on their shelves. Zoltanski, the city's first female mayor, said the ad trivialized violence against women and that the city -- which relies on the roughly $1 million a year the shop generates -- wants to stock brands with a more responsible message going forward, including from women-owned companies. Reaction among golfers has been mixed: most agree the ad was wrong, but some told KSL that pulling merchandise may be too harsh a response.
item.dc:creator: Garna Mejia, KSL

item.title: Man paralyzed saving child gets Utah and global support
item.description: Josh Collette, 42, suffered a complete cervical spinal cord injury that left him paralyzed from the neck down after diving into a rip current off Riviera Beach in San Clemente, California, on Aug. 15 to rescue an 8-year-old boy. His family says the injury has kept him unable to breathe or speak on his own, and doctors have told them a full recovery, including walking again, is unlikely. More than 1,000 donors from the U.S. and abroad have contributed over $400,000 to a GoFundMe for his care, and his daughter Grace said the outpouring of support from strangers has been striking. In Utah, Collette's cousin Brooke Higley, owner of Sweet Street Bakery in Herriman, held a Saturday bake sale that she estimated would raise about $2,000 for the family. Relatives describe Collette as someone who has always shown up for others and say they're now watching that same spirit returned to him by people who never met him.
item.dc:creator: Tyrese Boone, KSL

item.title: Inflation and the economy are top issues for Utah voters heading into the midterms
item.description: A Deseret News/Hinckley Institute of Politics poll conducted by Morning Consult found that 48% of Utah voters cited the economy and jobs, and 41% cited inflation, as the issues that would most affect their midterm vote, far outpacing corruption (27%), immigration (23%) and family values (23%).
