The survey of 789 registered voters, taken Aug. 6-11 with a margin of error of about 3 points, also found growing uncertainty about which party voters will back: those saying they'd vote almost entirely Republican dropped from 43% to 39% while Democratic-leaning voters ticked up from 28% to 31%, and the share unsure of their choice roughly doubled to 14%. Hinckley Institute director Jason Perry said the shift doesn't signal a major partisan realignment since Republicans still hold a clear edge, but he called the rising number of undecided voters a notable data point given how close control of Congress is heading into November.
item.dc:creator: Cami Mondeaux, Deseret News

item.title: St. George Fire Department to hold stair climb remembering 25 years since attacks on 9/11
item.description: To mark 25 years since the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks, the St. George Fire Department and the city are hosting a 9/11 Stair Climb Challenge at the Stairs at Tech Ridge, with participants climbing five flights repeatedly to match the 110 flights firefighters climbed in the World Trade Center towers. Deputy Chief Brad Esplin, who recalled watching the second plane hit while in a college class in 2001, said the annual tradition honors the 343 firefighters killed that day and is open to the whole community, not just first responders. The event runs 8-10 p.m., costs $20.01 to commemorate the year of the attacks, and currently has more than 100 of a roughly 350-person registration cap filled; spectators can watch for free from bleachers.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Early-morning flight to Salt Lake City set to return to Pocatello Airport
item.description: Pocatello Regional Airport will regain a near-daily early-morning flight to Salt Lake City starting Oct. 2, after Delta restructured its schedule and handed the route back to regional carrier SkyWest, according to airport manager Alan Evans. The airport lost the early flight about a year ago when Delta pulled it for reasons tied to bookings and profitability, and Evans said many residents had asked for its return since it's important for business and leisure travelers needing schedule flexibility. He said fares will be more competitive with those out of Idaho Falls and could even undercut the cost of driving to Salt Lake City to fly, but cautioned that keeping the route depends on the community actually filling seats.
item.dc:creator: Logan Ramsey, EastIdahoNews.com

item.title: Historic Tenth Ward Square offers glimpse into changing Church of Jesus Christ chapel designs
item.description: Tenth Ward Square in Salt Lake City traces back to an 1853 adobe chapel built the same year construction began on the Salt Lake Temple, and has been rebuilt and expanded several times since, including a brick chapel finished in 1873 and a larger 1909-1916 building that's now the site's centerpiece. Historic sites curator Emily Utt told KSL the 1909 chapel features an organ, a stained-glass window of Christ knocking at a door, and a balcony reached by a winding staircase, and that President Gordon B. Hinckley once worshipped there. A 1997-2000 renovation combined the original chapel, an 1887 schoolhouse and the 1909 building into a single accessible meetinghouse, adding modern touches like air conditioning and a sound system while preserving the 1909 chapel's original look; a time capsule from the chapel's cornerstone was also opened and its contents displayed. Utt called it one of her favorite buildings for showing the evolution of Latter-day Saint worship on a single block since the city's founding.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Utah nurse prescribes something extra: Opera
item.description: Luiz Meneghin, a nurse at Aspen Ridge Transitional Rehabilitation in Murray, sings opera for his mostly elderly patients three times a week, a practice rooted in a childhood love of music he developed growing up poor in Brazil and later channeled into voice lessons and a 2012 appearance on "America's Got Talent." Beyond his nursing job, he's writing a movie script and has published a children's book, "The Hairy King," adapted from stories he told his own kids. During performances at the facility's Midvale location, he sings pieces like "Ave Maria," "O Sole Mio" and "Nessun dorma" using a portable stereo as his "orchestra," saying music helps patients feel like they're somewhere other than a care center. He was moved to learn that a patient who died had listed his singing among her favorite things in an obituary.
item.dc:creator: Peter Rosen, KSL

item.title: Are mortgage rates creeping up again?
item.description: The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate ticked up slightly to 6.6% this week, according to Freddie Mac, ending two straight weeks of declines but still below year-ago levels; Mortgage News Daily's tracker showed a similar small increase to 6.75%. The Wall Street Journal reported rates aren't likely to drop much soon, pointing to inflation pressure from the ongoing U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran, which halted a brief dip below 6% seen earlier this year. A new Salt Lake Board of Realtors report blamed geopolitical tension and inflation data for the recent rate spike and said the combination with limited housing supply and high development costs is worsening affordability; it estimated that a rate drop from 6.41% to 5.41% would cut the income needed to afford a typical Salt Lake County home from about $187,000 to roughly $172,000.
item.dc:creator: Lisa Riley Roche, Deseret News

item.title: Floods strike homes in Emery County
item.description: Heavy rain triggered flooding across Emery County on Saturday, damaging multiple homes and roads and prompting the Emery County Sheriff's Office to open a Red Cross shelter at an LDS meetinghouse in Orangeville for displaced residents. The National Weather Service issued flood warnings for parts of Carbon, Emery, Sanpete and Kane counties, with flash flood warnings in Kane County lasting until 10:45 p.m., and urged residents from St. George to Price to have backup plans for outdoor activities. The same storm system flipped 34 railcars near Lynndyl in Millard County and uprooted trees that damaged homes, according to Sheriff Steve O'Camb, whose office was still assessing damage as of the report.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: 3 killed in Duchesne County after head-on collision with semi
item.description: Three people died Friday afternoon when a semitruck overcorrected after drifting off U.S. 40 near Duchesne and struck a guardrail, then crossed into oncoming traffic and hit a Kia hatchback head-on, according to the Utah Department of Public Safety. All three occupants of the Kia -- a 52-year-old woman driving, a 42-year-old man in the front seat and an 18-year-old man in back -- died on impact; none had been publicly identified as of the report. The semi driver was hospitalized with injuries that did not appear life-threatening.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Unregulated horse racing at Ogden facility, decried by PETA, has stopped, for now
item.description: Unregulated quarter-horse match racing at Weber County's Golden Spike Event Center, which PETA says has run since at least 2007, has stopped for now after the animal-rights group's investigation last April alleged drugging, whipping and shock-device abuse of horses. Golden Spike general manager Duncan Olsen defended the horse owners involved and disputed PETA's characterization, though the American Quarter Horse Association had separately urged Weber County in 2024 to stop allowing the unregulated events. Olsen said county officials want more information before permitting the races to resume, while PETA's Hannah Schein said some of the same stables have moved their races to Nevada and that she's now investigating possible unregulated racing at a track in Beryl, Iron County. Regulated Utah Quarter Horse Racing Association events at Golden Spike are continuing, with the next scheduled for Sept. 13.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: New poll: Inside the 2026 wildfire season and how Utahns feel about it
item.description: Utah's 2026 wildfire season -- 843 fires burning more than half a million acres and killing two firefighter pilots -- is on pace to be among the state's worst, and a Deseret News/Hinckley Institute poll found 93% of Utah voters are at least somewhat concerned about it. University of Utah professor Philip Dennison said this is the first year three individual fires have approached or topped 100,000 acres, and nearly half of poll respondents reported health symptoms like coughing or irritated eyes from smoke, with about two-thirds limiting outdoor time. Researchers separately found smoke-related air pollution and heat may be linked to a rise in suicides, and Dennison noted Utah will keep absorbing smoke from fires in neighboring states even if its own blazes are controlled. Gov. Spencer Cox issued a 30-day state of emergency on July 22 to speed wildfire funding, and the state had spent more than $100 million fighting fires as of July 31; poll respondents broadly supported more funding for public lands (63%) and stiffer penalties for fire-safety violations (73%). Dennison argued that hardening homes against embers and better identifying which fires can safely burn for ecological benefit, rather than suppressing all of them, are the more effective long-term strategies.
item.dc:creator: Leah Bowers, Deseret News

item.title: What's special about Westminster? New president Sylvia Torti is eager to offer answers
item.description: Sylvia Torti began her tenure as Westminster University's 20th president this week, replacing longtime president Beth Dobkin, and told the Deseret News she wants the 151-year-old Salt Lake City school known as a top "intentionally small" university built on a culture of collaboration. Torti, an Ohio native who earned her Ph.D. in biology at the University of Utah and later led the U.'s Honors College from 2012-2023 before running Maine's College of the Atlantic, said Westminster's community-based, relationship-driven education model and small Sugar House campus drew her back to Utah. University of Utah President Taylor Randall welcomed her return, citing her record on student success and engagement. Torti pointed to Westminster's high four-year graduation rate, a 90% job-or-grad-school placement rate for graduates, and its status as the state's only school offering a fully funded sophomore study-abroad program as reasons students should consider it, while also planning a capital campaign to expand scholarship funding.
item.dc:creator: Jason Swensen, Deseret News

item.title: Girl shoots, kills family member in Iron County, sheriff's office says
item.description: A 15-year-old girl fatally shot her mother, 45-year-old Mary Ellen Billings (also known as Mary Ellen Crase) of Kanarraville, early Saturday morning, according to the Iron County Sheriff's Office, which said deputies responding to a report on Main Street found Billings already dead and recovered a .38-caliber handgun at the scene. Officials have not released what led to the shooting and took the girl into custody; the sheriff's office called it an isolated incident with no threat to the community. Billings had recently spoken to KSL about Flock camera concerns near her home and described herself and her children as domestic violence survivors. The Iron County School District, which confirmed a student was involved, said its crisis response team would be on affected campuses Monday and pointed families to the SafeUT crisis line, along with state and national domestic violence hotlines.
item.dc:creator: Ashley Imlay, KSL

item.title: Goshute Indian tribe voices opposition to U.S. Army data center proposal in Tooele County
item.description: The Skull Valley Band of Goshute Indians, based in Grantsville, publicly opposed a U.S. Army data center proposed for 1,201 acres at Dugway Proving Ground in Tooele County, warning the facility's projected 500-megawatt power draw and up to 250,000 gallons a day of salt-heavy wastewater discharge would strain the region's already over-allocated groundwater, the tribe's only water source. The Army announced the project last March with Dallas-based developer CyrusOne, targeting completion by 2029 to support AI, drone-swarm and command-and-control computing, and has said an environmental review will precede construction; officials didn't respond to a request for comment. Tribal leaders, whose 134-member band covers about 28 square miles, sent Gov. Spencer Cox a letter of opposition that went unanswered and are asking Tooele County to reject related zoning requests. The tribe also separately opposes an EnergySolutions plan to import 1.31 million cubic yards of Canadian low-level radioactive waste to its nearby Clive facility, saying it hasn't been consulted despite being among the populations most exposed to any accident.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Weber County citizenship review verifies 99.6% of voters, finds three noncitizens
item.description: A months-long statewide review of voter rolls verified 99.6% of Weber County's 158,226 registered voters as U.S. citizens and identified three confirmed noncitizens, who were immediately removed -- one of whom had voted in 2018 -- according to Weber County Clerk/Auditor Ricky Hatch. Utah Democrats pointed to the low noncitizen count as evidence that fears about noncitizen voting are overblown, while Hatch cautioned that the roughly 634 voters whose citizenship couldn't be immediately confirmed are not necessarily noncitizens, often due to clerical errors or older registrations lacking modern ID data; those voters can cast federal-only ballots until verified. The county's results mirrored the state's broader review, which checked over 2 million records and found 99.72% verified, 27 confirmed noncitizens statewide and about 5,007 unconfirmed. Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson said the review both flagged vulnerabilities and helped protect eligible voters from wrongful removal, and Hatch said the findings show Weber County's rolls are cleaner than ever.
item.dc:creator: Eric Cabrera, KSL

item.title: Ogden woman became widowed by suicide, now she hosts events for singles adults to meet
item.description: Molly Bitton of Ogden turned to her running community for support after her husband died by suicide in March 2013 following years of addiction, leaving her a widow with two young children, and that experience later inspired her to create ways for single adults to meet in person. She started with a "singles mingle" 5K built around icebreaker games rather than competition, then expanded into a series of events called Have You Met? that have included volleyball, Utah Jazz games, pickleball and an upcoming comedy show and walk-and-talk, drawing guest speakers like Damona Hoffman from the Drew Barrymore show. Bitton said she launched the events partly out of frustration with dating apps, and while she isn't currently looking for a relationship herself, she wants to offer others the same safe, connecting space her running community gave her during grief.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Could Oura Rings provide clues to Cottonwood Heights man's missing remains?
item.description: Jennifer Gledhill, 43, is charged with murder in the 2024 disappearance and presumed death of her estranged husband, Matthew Johnson, a 51-year-old member of U.S. Special Operations who went missing in late September 2024 after prosecutors say she shot him. New search warrants show investigators examined data from an Oura Ring Gledhill was wearing on the day of the alleged killing, along with location data suggesting she disposed of evidence the next day. Court documents also describe home surveillance cameras Johnson had installed, through which he allegedly discovered her infidelity before his death. Salt Lake County District Attorney Sim Gill said the case remains under active investigation, and Johnson's remains have not been found. Gledhill's trial is scheduled to begin Dec. 7.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy

item.title: St. George residents asked to limit power use as city enters 'red alert' after outage
item.description: St. George declared a power "red alert" Friday after a Rocky Mountain Power outage tied to a PacifiCorp regional transformer problem knocked out electricity to more than 14,000 customers starting Thursday evening, with some outages continuing into Friday. City crews have been restoring power in stages to avoid overloading the grid while keeping critical services online. Officials are asking residents to cut back on electricity use between 3 and 7 p.m., the window when solar output drops and evening demand peaks, and to hold off on running dishwashers and laundry machines until after 7 p.m. Emergency diesel generators are staged and ready to deploy if the situation worsens.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown

item.title: Longtime judge and an attorney appointed to 2 seats on Utah Supreme Court
item.description: Gov. Spencer Cox announced Friday that he is appointing 5th District Judge Matthew Bell and Salt Lake City attorney Michael Menssen to fill two vacancies on the Utah Supreme Court. Bell, a judge since 2017 and former U.S. Department of Justice attorney, and Menssen, a commercial litigation partner at Mayer Brown, would replace retired Chief Justice Matthew Durrant and resigned Justice Diana Hagen. Both nominees still need confirmation by the state Senate, and Cox said he expects to name a new chief justice within six to eight weeks. This marks Cox's fifth appointment to the state's high court since it expanded to seven seats last October.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko and Daniel Woodruff

item.title: Challenge encourages Utahns to keep Jordan River clean
item.description: Mayors from cities along the Jordan River have launched a yearlong "Love Your Watershed" challenge asking residents across the three counties and 16 cities the river runs through to keep litter and debris out of storm drains and gutters. Jordan River Commission representative Rachel Lyn said the effort is meant to remind people that whatever goes down a storm drain ultimately reaches the river. The campaign is timed around the Get to the River Festival in September, which includes more than 50 free events plus a dedicated cleanup service day on Sept. 11. Organizers are directing residents to jordanrivercommission.gov for details on how to get involved.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer

item.title: Utahns with ties to Nepal react to deadly flooding
item.description: Deadly flooding along Nepal's northern border with China has killed hundreds of people and left more than 1,000 missing, and Utahns with ties to the country are reacting with alarm. Dean Cardinale, founder of World Wide Trekking and the humanitarian nonprofit Human Outreach Project, said the scale of the disaster is heartbreaking given his decades of trekking and aid work in Nepal, and he plans to return within about a month to help assess recovery needs. Sunil Pandey, a Nepal native now living in Utah who founded the Asian Community Development Center, is struggling to reach missing family and friends because of communication breakdowns in the affected region. Cardinale noted that events like this are hard to forecast and control, comparing it to the flash flooding Utah sometimes sees.
item.dc:creator: Shelby Lofton

item.title: Driver accused of causing head-on crash faces a dozen charges
item.description: Jonathan Casimiro Abarca-Rodriguez, 26, of Salt Lake City faces 12 charges after prosecutors say he crossed into oncoming lanes on Route 248 near Park City on Aug. 22 and struck another vehicle head-on, injuring four people. Charging documents say his preliminary breath test measured 0.277% blood-alcohol content, more than five times the legal limit, and that he fled the scene with a passenger before being found in a nearby field. He faces counts including leaving the scene of a serious-injury accident, negligent operation causing injury, driving without a required interlock device as an alcohol-restricted driver, and an open-container violation. Court records show he was previously convicted of DUI in April 2025.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy

item.title: Police in Herriman offer back-to-school reminder about new Utah e-bike law
item.description: Herriman police joined administrators at Providence Hall Junior High this week to brief students and parents on Utah's e-bike law, which took effect May 6 and requires riders under 21 to wear helmets while treating higher-powered e-motorcycles as vehicles that require a driver's license. Operations Commander Marcus Beckstead said the outreach is a safety response to a wave of injuries and deaths involving e-devices, with more than 1,100 crashes and 35 deaths reported statewide this year. Intermountain Primary Children's Hospital has also seen a 66.7% jump in e-bike injuries among kids and teens, and only about 40% of those injured were wearing helmets. Next year's law will add a requirement that riders ages 8 to 15 either ride with adult supervision or complete an online safety course, and Herriman police said they plan to shift from education toward enforcement.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams

item.title: MOOYAH expanding Utah presence with 6 new locations
item.description: Texas-based burger chain MOOYAH plans to add six new Utah locations, growing beyond its current four restaurants in Provo, Riverton, Sandy and South Jordan. Franchisees Art and Nick Depole will develop new sites in St. George and Davis County along with additional locations in markets where the chain already operates. MOOYAH, known for made-to-order burgers, fries and shakes, first entered Utah with its Provo restaurant in 2016 and now operates more than 80 locations nationwide. Art Depole said Utah's consumer landscape has offered clear opportunities for the brand's growth.

item.title: Fall is almost here. Is this when Utah's spectacular colors will return?
item.description: KSL Weather forecasters expect Utah's mountain fall foliage to peak between late September and early October, with valley colors following in October. Meteorologist Matt Johnson said reaching vibrant colors depends on warm, sunny days paired with cool, dry nights, and near-normal or below-normal temperatures could help trigger the change this year. Drought, record summer heat and recent wildfires have stressed trees, leading University of Utah professor David Bowling to say it's genuinely unclear how the season will play out. Utah State University forest ecologist Darren McAvoy said he remains optimistic despite the unusual conditions.
